## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}
\end{marginfigure}

_*What happens computationally during a single model invocation, how does hardware constrain its latency and throughput, and what software contract must the runtime enforce to govern it safely?*_

Traditional computer systems rely on deterministic, fail-stop processors: instructions execute exactly as written, invalid memory accesses trigger hardware traps, and execution state is inspectable. A foundation model violates all of these invariants. It evaluates probability distributions over discrete subword integers, emits candidate strings without modifying host state, and cannot verify whether its own output is correct. Treating the model as a conversational partner leads to silent corruptions, resource exhaustion, and security failures. Building reliable agent infrastructure requires formalizing the model invocation boundary: bounding its token and latency budgets, understanding the memory-bandwidth physics of single-batch autoregressive decode, constraining output syntax at decode time via grammar logit masking, and wrapping candidate proposals in deterministic host verification.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Contrast the execution model of a classical deterministic CPU with that of an unprivileged generative model operating under Zero Ambient Authority ($A=0$).
- Explain Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) as statistical data serialization, demonstrating the impedance mismatch between statistical subwords and programming language ASTs.
- Trace the autoregressive execution loop, showing why next-token generation forms an irreducibly serial causal dependency chain on accelerator memory ($O(K)$ serialization).
- Diagnose invocation latency and throughput using the Accelerator Roofline Model, quantitatively distinguishing compute-bound prefill (GEMM) from memory-bandwidth-bound decode (GEMV) at $B=1$.
- Explain grammar-constrained decoding via decode-time logit masking at the execution surface, distinguishing syntactic validity from semantic correctness.
- Specify a typed model invocation contract with explicit token/deadline limits, streaming early cancellation (`RST_STREAM`), and a normalized status envelope.
- Decouple statistical sequence likelihood and text fluency from operational truth, defining the host runtime's external in-memory verification perimeter.
- Evaluate invocation interface designs (free-form markdown, JSON schema, and search/replace diffs) by syntax error rates, token overhead, latency, and verified task completion.

:::

## The Model Invocation Boundary {#sec-vol3-processor-role}

In classical computer systems architecture, the central processing unit is a deterministic, fail-stop execution engine. As codified across decades of instruction set architectures, a physical microprocessor executes a formal contract: machine instructions advance a program counter, mutate dedicated register files, alter memory locations governed by a hardware memory management unit, and trigger immediate hardware traps whenever execution encounters an illegal opcode, an unaligned bus access, or a memory protection violation. When an x86 or ARM processor executes an invalid instruction sequence, it halts deterministically, raising a fault that transfers control to a supervisor trap handler in operating system kernel space. Every state transition is observable, bounded by formal register transfer logic, and governed by invariant mechanical rules.

A foundation model operating as a processing element in an agentic system completely inverts this classical contract. The generative model is not an instruction set processor; it is a high-dimensional, parameterized non-linear function approximator. Its state is encapsulated entirely within static weight matrices, its input is a discrete sequence of integer tokens, and its computational cycle consists of mapping those input tokens through multi-head attention mechanisms and feed-forward networks on accelerator silicon to produce an unnormalized probability distribution over a discrete vocabulary. The model contains no internal program counter to advance sequential logic, no register file to hold temporary variables across distinct requests, no memory management unit to enforce address bounds, and no native hardware trap mechanism to intercept erroneous reasoning. It does not execute a program; it estimates the conditional probability of subsequent subword units given an arbitrary preceding token sequence.

Because the model lacks a physical address bus and direct execution privileges, its raw emissions possess zero ambient authority ($A=0$). When an autoregressive decode loop generates the character string `DROP TABLE users;` or `rm -rf /`, precisely zero bytes on physical persistent storage are mutated, and zero kernel system calls are initiated. The candidate token sequence resides purely in volatile host memory as an unverified byte buffer held in escrow. In the architecture of an agentic computer, the foundation model functions as an unprivileged, untrusted coprocessor operating within an absolute software sandbox. The host agent runtime serves as the authoritative operating system supervisor, maintaining complete mediation over every external boundary, staging all context inputs, dictating token and wall-clock execution limits, and determining whether candidate proposals are parsed, validated against formal schemas, or discarded without consequence.

To reason about this unprivileged coprocessor using the rigorous vocabulary of systems design, software engineers must discard colloquial anthropomorphisms and translate machine learning jargon into exact systems architecture primitives. The terms popularized by natural language processing literature—prompts, generation loops, logits, and hallucinations—describe concrete hardware data paths, statistical distributions, and software failure modes, as formalized in @tbl-vol3-ml-systems-rosetta.

| Machine Learning Abstraction | Systems Architecture Primitive | Operational Boundary & Semantic Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Prompt / Context Window** | Staged Input Buffer | A bounded, immutable array of discrete token identifiers staged in host memory, representing the entire observable state space passed across the invocation boundary for a single forward pass. |
| **Tokenization / BPE** | Subword Byte Serializer | A lossy statistical encoder-decoder mapping unstructured UTF-8 byte streams into fixed-width integer tokens, imposing an impedance mismatch against formal programming language grammars. |
| **Autoregressive Generation** | Iterative Sampling Loop | A serialized execution pipeline that repeatedly evaluates accelerator matrix kernels to sample a single token from a conditional probability distribution, appending it to the input buffer for the next iteration. |
| **Logits & Softmax** | Unnormalized Density Vector | A raw floating-point vector emitted by the final linear projection layer, exponentiated and normalized to define a categorical probability distribution over the vocabulary space. |
| **Hallucination / Confabulation** | Fail-Plausible State Corruption | An undetected operational failure where the statistical sampler emits semantically invalid, non-existent, or counterfactual assertions that exhibit high surface likelihood under the training distribution. |
| **Tool Call Proposal** | Unprivileged RPC Message Escrow | A candidate serialized remote procedure call payload emitted into host memory, carrying zero execution authority until parsed, type-checked, and dispatched by the supervisor runtime. |
| **HTTP 200 OK Response** | Transport-Layer Socket Closure | A transport protocol confirmation verifying solely that the network connection remained open and the inference daemon reached a termination condition, establishing zero guarantees of task success. |
: The Systems Architecture Rosetta Stone: Translating Machine Learning Terminology into Systems Primitives. {#tbl-vol3-ml-systems-rosetta}

The fundamental tension governing the model invocation boundary is the epistemic gap separating training likelihood from operational correctness. Classical hardware components and traditional software libraries are designed around fail-stop semantics: a failed checksum aborts a network packet, a missing symbol terminates a link-editor pass, and a division by zero raises a hardware exception. Generative foundation models, by contrast, exhibit fail-plausible behavior. Because the neural network is optimized via cross-entropy loss to minimize the negative log-likelihood of tokens drawn from human corpora, its objective function rewards textual coherence, syntactic elegance, and conversational fluency above empirical truth.

When presented with an underspecified problem, a missing system dependency, or an impossible logical constraint, the model does not halt with an error code. Instead, its sampling loop selects tokens that maximize surface plausibility, confidently emitting syntactically valid code that invokes fabricated library routines, hallucinates non-existent filesystem paths, or returns invalid parameter flags. The model is statistically incapable of distinguishing between an assertion that is true in the physical world and an assertion that merely mimics the stylistic cadences of a true statement. Sequence likelihood is not a proxy for operational validity; high-confidence emissions frequently mask total semantic failure.

To isolate this fail-plausible behavior and construct a dependable computing system around an undependable coprocessor, production agent systems implement a strict two-tier topology, separating supervisory control from accelerator execution. This separation of concerns, illustrated in @fig-stochastic-processor-core, divides the host execution environment from the neural inference server.

::: {#fig-stochastic-processor-core}
```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     HOST AGENT RUNTIME (CPU Supervisor)               |
|                                                                       |
|   +-------------------+   +--------------------+   +--------------+   |
|   | Context Staging & |   | Token Accounting & |   | Static AST   |   |
|   | Prefix Alignment  |   | Latency Budgets    |   | Verifiers    |   |
|   +---------+---------+   +---------+----------+   +-------^------+   |
|             |                       |                      |          |
+-------------|-----------------------|----------------------|----------+
              | RPC Invocation Buffer | Explicit Contract    | Escrow
              | (Staged Tokens, Temp) | (Budgets, Stop Cond) | Result
+-------------|-----------------------|----------------------|----------+
|             v                       v                      |          |
|   +--------------------------------------------------------+------+   |
|   |               INFERENCE SERVING DAEMON (vLLM / SGLang)        |   |
|   |   - Continuous Batching Engine    - KV Cache Memory Manager   |   |
|   |   - Grammar Bitmask Interceptor   - Sampling Scheduler        |   |
|   +---------------------------------+-----------------------------+   |
|                                     | Matrix Kernel Dispatch
|                                     v (GEMM Prefill / GEMV Decode)
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |               NEURAL ACCELERATOR CORE (GPU / HBM)             |   |
|   |   - Model Weights (Theta) in High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM)       |   |
|   |   - Tensor Cores / Systolic Matrix Multiplication Units       |   |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------+   |

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The Two-Tier Stochastic Computer Architecture. The Host Agent Runtime on the CPU maintains complete supervisory authority, staging context and verifying outputs, while the Inference Serving Tier coordinates accelerator hardware to evaluate token sequences without ambient execution privilege.
:::

In this topology, the host agent runtime executes on general-purpose CPU cores, owning the primary task state, orchestrating context memory assembly, enforcing token budgets, and executing deterministic validation passes such as Abstract Syntax Tree parsing and schema conformance checks. Beneath the host runtime sits the inference serving daemon—typically an optimized serving engine such as vLLM or SGLang—which manages batch scheduling, coordinates physical memory allocations for intermediate attention states, and compiles grammar constraints into logit bitmasks. At the lowest tier lies the neural accelerator hardware itself, consisting of tensor compute engines and High-Bandwidth Memory storing the static model weights $\Theta$. Information crosses the boundary from the host to the inference engine solely as a structured remote procedure call payload, and candidate tokens return across that same boundary into host memory escrow. At no point does the accelerator tier execute instructions on the host system or bypass the supervisor's mediation layer.

The existence of this structured communication link exposes a critical systems pitfall: the Delivery Fallacy. In standard client-server network programming, an `HTTP 200 OK` status indicates that a requested operation completed successfully. At the model invocation boundary, however, an `HTTP 200 OK` response indicates only that the transport-layer connection remained healthy, the JSON payload was properly formatted, and the serving daemon's autoregressive decode loop reached an explicit stop sequence or token limit without encountering a driver crash. The status code establishes absolutely nothing regarding the syntactic integrity, logical consistency, or operational correctness of the generated content. A response containing a broken JSON payload, an invalid tool name, a hallucinated git command, or malicious shell injection syntax arrives wrapped inside the identical `HTTP 200 OK` transport envelope as an optimal task plan.

Treating transport delivery as task success is a catastrophic architectural error. The host agent runtime must enforce a defense-in-depth posture that treats every model emission as unverified user input. Before any candidate sequence is permitted to leave escrow and influence downstream system state, it must clear a battery of static verification gates executed entirely within host memory: JSON deserialization against strict schemas, Abstract Syntax Tree validation against target programming language grammars, and range checking against permitted runtime capabilities. Only when these deterministic filters pass without error does the host supervisor promote a candidate emission from an unprivileged string to an actionable system event.

Building such a supervisory architecture requires understanding the precise mechanics through which continuous neural networks interface with discrete computational systems. Before an inference engine can evaluate a single matrix transformation, and before the host runtime can inspect a generated token sequence, arbitrary text must be transformed across the discrete boundary separating human language from accelerator memory. This translation is governed by discrete tokenization—a statistical byte serialization process whose mechanical idiosyncrasies directly shape sequence length, inference latency, and the fundamental impedance mismatch between natural language models and formal programming language syntax.

## Discrete Tokenization and Sequence Representation {#sec-vol3-processor-tokenization}

A foundation model cannot process continuous strings, ASCII streams, or arbitrary byte buffers directly; its underlying tensor engines operate exclusively over discrete sequences of numerical vectors residing in accelerator memory. Before a model can evaluate a single layer of attention or emit a single token continuation, human-readable text must cross a discrete translation boundary. This translation is governed by **tokenization**—a deterministic, statistical byte serialization process that maps raw byte sequences to discrete integer identifiers drawn from a finite vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$, and subsequently gathers dense vector representations from an accelerator-resident embedding table.

In computer systems engineering, the choice of data serialization format directly dictates processing throughput, memory bus utilization, and structural alignment across subsystem interfaces. Tokenization is not an abstract linguistic exercise; it is the physical input/output serialization protocol of the neural processing unit. For an autonomous agent runtime operating in the dual-tier topology, the mechanical idiosyncrasies of this serialization layer introduce fundamental systems challenges: severe impedance mismatches with compiler Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), significant token-inflation taxes on structured remote procedure calls (RPCs), and catastrophic truncation failure modes when generation bounds are exceeded.

### The Lexing Boundary: Why Compilers and Neural Networks Disagree

In traditional compiler design, lexical analysis is a solved problem. A lexer constructed via deterministic finite automata (DFAs)—such as those generated by `flex` or embedded in tree-sitter grammars—scans an input character stream and partitions it into typed lexical tokens: identifiers, keywords (`def`, `return`), numeric literals, and punctuation operators. The lexer operates over a formal grammar with strict, context-free or regular rules. Whitespace is either discarded as non-semantic trivia or transformed into unambiguous indentation tokens (`INDENT`, `DEDENT`) that govern block scope.

Large language models cannot employ traditional compiler lexers for two primary systems reasons:

1. **The Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) Bottleneck of Word-Level Models:** If an engine tokenized text at the natural word or programming identifier level, the vocabulary size $|\mathcal{V}|$ would become unbounded. In open-vocabulary codebases, developers create arbitrary identifier names (`camelCaseFunctionName_v2`), serialize raw SHA-256 hashes, and manipulate hex dumps. A word-level vocabulary must either grow to millions of entries—destroying memory efficiency—or map unrecognized sequences to an out-of-vocabulary marker (`<unk>`), destroying critical semantic entropy.
2. **The Quadratic Attention Penalty of Raw Byte/Character Sequences:** At the opposite extreme, tokenizing at the level of individual ASCII characters or raw bytes ($|\mathcal{V}| = 256$) eliminates the OOV problem entirely. However, character-level representation causes the sequence length $S$ to expand by a factor of $4\times$ to $6\times$ relative to standard natural language text or code. Because the full-context attention mechanism has computational complexity that scales quadratically with sequence length ($O(S^2)$), a $4\times$ inflation in sequence length increases the floating-point operations of attention by $16\times$ and exhausts context-window capacity prematurely.

To resolve this tension between vocabulary explosion and sequence length inflation, modern inference serving systems standardize on **subword tokenization**, predominantly implemented via **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)** with a byte-level fallback.

```
       RAW UTF-8 BYTE STREAM               SUBWORD MERGE TABLE               DISCRETE TOKEN SEQUENCE
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────────┐     ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ "def get_user_id(db):"        │ ──> │ 1. 'u' + 's' -> 'us'        │ ──> │ [755, 3452, 1987, 856, 1289]   │
  │ (20 bytes, hex: 64 65 66 ...) │     │ 2. 'e' + 'r' -> 'er'        │     │ (5 discrete integer IDs)      │
  └───────────────────────────────┘     │ 3. 'us' + 'er' -> 'user'    │     └───────────────────────────────┘
                                        └─────────────────────────────┘
```

BPE is a greedy compression algorithm (originally developed for data compression by Philip Gage in 1994) adapted as a statistical vocabulary compiler. The tokenizer construction proceeds through two distinct phases:

* **Offline Vocabulary Compilation:** The tokenizer starts with a base vocabulary consisting of all 256 possible single-byte values, guaranteeing that any byte stream can be parsed without OOV failures. Over a massive pre-training corpus, the algorithm counts the frequency of all adjacent byte or subword pairs. The most frequent pair $(c_i, c_j)$ is merged into a new, discrete vocabulary entry $c_{\text{new}}$. This merge operation is recorded in a priority-ordered merge table, and the process repeats iteratively until the vocabulary reaches a predetermined size $|\mathcal{V}|$ (typically $32{,}000 \le |\mathcal{V}| \le 256{,}000$).
* **Online Sequence Tokenization:** When tokenizing text during agent inference, the tokenizer reads the input string as a byte sequence and greedily applies the compiled merge rules in priority order. Common words, syntactic keywords, and frequent code idioms are compressed into single discrete token IDs, while rare variable names or arbitrary cryptographic hashes are split into shorter subwords or fallback individual bytes.

While BPE provides a mathematically balanced compression ratio (averaging roughly 3.5 to 4.2 characters per token across common English text), it is purely statistical and syntax-blind. It operates with zero awareness of programming language grammar, scope hierarchies, or identifier boundaries.

### The Accelerator Memory Boundary: Embedding Tables as Vector Gather Engines

Once the tokenizer transforms a raw string into a sequence of $M$ discrete integer token IDs $\mathbf{t} = [t_1, t_2, \dots, t_M]$, where each $t_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, |\mathcal{V}| - 1\}$, the integer vector must be transferred to accelerator High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to initialize model computation.

In foundational machine learning literature, the embedding step is frequently expressed as the matrix multiplication of a one-hot vector $\mathbf{e}_i \in \{0, 1\}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$ by an embedding weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d_{\text{model}}}$:

$$\mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}$$ {#eq-one-hot-embedding}

In a production systems environment, @eq-one-hot-embedding is a mathematical fiction. No physical accelerator allocates a sparse vector with $|\mathcal{V}| - 1$ zeros or dispatches a matrix multiplication kernel against a vector of 128,000 components to select a single row.

On physical hardware, token IDs function strictly as **memory address offsets** for a parallel vector gather operation. The accelerator runtime treats the embedding table $\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}$ as a contiguous two-dimensional array allocated in HBM. For each input token $t_i$, the GPU memory controller calculates the physical memory address of the corresponding row:

$$\text{Address}(t_i) = \text{BaseAddress}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}) + \Big(t_i \times d_{\text{model}} \times \text{sizeof}(\text{dtype})\Big)$$ {#eq-embed-address}

The accelerator dispatches a memory gather kernel that reads $d_{\text{model}}$ contiguous floating-point values (typically 16-bit `float16` or `bfloat16`, consuming 2 bytes per element) from HBM into the on-chip register file and Static RAM (SRAM) of the Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). This operation forms the initial activation tensor $\mathbf{X}^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d_{\text{model}}}$.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Sizing the Embedding Table in Accelerator Memory"}
Consider a modern 70-billion parameter foundation model (such as Llama 3 70B) deployed on an NVIDIA H100 GPU:
- Vocabulary size: $|\mathcal{V}| = 128{,}256$
- Hidden dimension: $d_{\text{model}} = 8{,}192$
- Numerical representation: BF16 ($\text{sizeof}(\text{dtype}) = 2\text{ bytes}$)

We calculate the physical memory footprint of the input embedding table $\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}$ in accelerator HBM:

$$\text{Footprint}_{\text{embed}} = |\mathcal{V}| \times d_{\text{model}} \times \text{sizeof}(\text{dtype})$$

$$\text{Footprint}_{\text{embed}} = 128{,}256 \times 8{,}192 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 2{,}101{,}346{,}304\text{ bytes} \approx 1.957\text{ GiB}$$

If the serving system maintains an untied language model head (where the final output de-embedding projection matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\text{unembed}}$ does not share physical memory with $\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}$), the input and output translation layers collectively consume:

$$\text{Footprint}_{\text{total\_vocab}} = 2 \times 1.957\text{ GiB} = 3.914\text{ GiB}$$

Nearly $4\text{ GiB}$ of high-bandwidth memory is allocated strictly to translating between discrete integer offsets and dense activation vectors before a single attention or feed-forward layer is evaluated.
:::

The sheer size of $\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}$ highlights why vocabulary sizes are tightly constrained in accelerator design. Expanding $|\mathcal{V}|$ from $128\text{k}$ to $256\text{k}$ to reduce sequence length directly claims an additional $2\text{ GiB}$ of HBM per table, directly reducing the memory capacity available for the runtime's dynamic key-value caches.

### The AST Impedance Mismatch and Fractured Semantics

Because BPE vocabulary construction is driven entirely by statistical character frequencies rather than formal grammars, token boundaries do not align with programming language AST nodes. This structural disconnect is known as the **AST Impedance Mismatch**.

When a software compiler parses an identifier such as `fetch_user_credentials`, the lexer treats the entire identifier as an atomic syntactic entity. In contrast, a subword tokenizer breaks this identifier into arbitrary statistical fragments: `['fetch', '_user', '_cred', 'entials']`. Each fragment is assigned an independent token ID and mapped to a completely distinct row in $\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}$.

The systems implications of this mismatch are particularly severe when handling **source code indentation** and **syntactic whitespace**. In Python, indentation defines block scope and control flow. However, BPE tokenizers greedily merge whitespace with adjacent characters based on corpus co-occurrence statistics, creating disjoint representations for identical semantic keywords.

Consider what occurs in a model's embedding layer when tokenizing the Python keyword `def` at column 0 versus column 4 (indented inside a class definition):

```
Case A: Unindented (Column 0)
Source Text:    "def calculate():"
Token IDs:      [755, 14820, 290]
Token Strings:  ["def", " calculate", "():"]

Case B: Indented by 4 Spaces (Column 4)
Source Text:    "    def calculate():"
Token IDs:      [220, 711, 14820, 290]  (or fused token [8129, 14820, 290])
Token Strings:  ["    ", " def", " calculate", "():"]
```

Under Case A, the keyword `def` is encoded as token ID `755`. Under Case B, the presence of four leading spaces causes the tokenizer to emit token ID `220` (representing four spaces) followed by token ID `711` (representing a space fused with the letters `def`), or in some tokenizers, a single fused token ID `8129` representing `    def`.

```
Tree-Sitter Clean AST:
   FunctionDef
   ├── name: "calculate"
   ├── parameters: ()
   └── body: Block

BPE Tokenization Stream:
   Column 0: [ Token 755: "def" ] ─────────> HBM Row 755 (Vector A)
   Column 4: [ Token 711: " def" ] ────────> HBM Row 711 (Vector B)
             (Zero shared identity at the physical embedding boundary)
```
*Figure 2.1: The AST Impedance Mismatch. The formal compiler parses an identical function definition keyword, whereas the statistical tokenizer emits distinct integer IDs that map to completely disjoint, orthogonal vectors in accelerator HBM.* {#fig-token-ast-mismatch}

In accelerator HBM, row `755` ($\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}[755]$) and row `711` ($\mathbf{W}_{\text{embed}}[711]$) are independent floating-point vectors. At the physical input boundary, the neural coprocessor receives two orthogonal vectors that share zero identity bits. The model must dedicate significant parameter capacity across multiple internal transformer layers simply to learn the invariant that Vector A and Vector B represent the identical Python keyword under different horizontal offsets.

This impedance mismatch produces observable failure modes in production agent systems:

1. **Identifier Mutation Under Renaming:** When an agent attempts an automated refactoring task, altering a variable name from `temp_cache` to `temporary_cache` alters the subword partitioning of the entire statement. The downstream token alignments change, occasionally causing the model to mispredict subsequent punctuation, missing parentheses, or generating syntax errors in code sections it did not intend to modify.
2. **Brittle Diff Generation:** Software agents that emit standard line-based unified diffs (`@@ -14,6 +14,7 @@`) frequently generate malformed hunks. The model must calculate line-count offsets and patch markers through subwords, where numbers and whitespace are fractured unpredictably, frequently failing verification in external host linters.

### The Serialization Tax on Structured Tool Calls

Autonomous agents do not interact with the host environment through unconstrained natural language; they operate via structured protocols such as JSON-RPC, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and direct CLI execution. When the host runtime prompts an agent to invoke a tool, the invocation payload is typically serialized as a JSON object containing the target function name and an argument map.

JSON is an exceptionally poor serialization format for autoregressive tokenizers. It imposes a massive **serialization tax**—a substantial inflation in the number of tokens required to convey a unit of functional intent. This inflation arises from three compounding factors:

* **Structural Boilerplate:** JSON requires repetitive structural tokens: double quotes around every key name (`"name"`, `"arguments"`), colons, commas, and curly braces. Each structural marker consumes one or more discrete token IDs.
* **Whitespace and Formatting Overhead:** Standard JSON serializers emit newlines and multi-space indentations for readability. When an agent emits pretty-printed JSON, it consumes dozens of tokens solely advancing the cursor across indentation levels.
* **String Escaping Multipliers:** When a tool call takes an argument that is itself source code or a terminal shell command, JSON requires escaping double quotes (`\"`), backslashes (`\\`), and newlines (`\n`). In BPE tokenizers, backslash escaping routinely breaks common subword merges. A sequence like `print("hello\n")` transforms into an escaped string where every backslash and escaped quote is isolated into an individual byte fallback token, inflating the token count of the payload by $30\%$ to $50\%$.

The following schema illustrates a standard tool invocation dispatched by an agent runtime:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ToolCallEnvelope:
    call_id: str
    tool_name: str
    arguments: Dict[str, Any]

# Canonical host-side invocation payload
raw_invocation = ToolCallEnvelope(
    call_id="call_98124_x",
    tool_name="write_file",
    arguments={
        "path": "src/auth/jwt.py",
        "content": "def decode_token(token: str) -> dict:\n    return jwt.decode(token, secret, algorithms=['HS256'])\n"
    }
)
```

When serialized to standard JSON for transmission across the model interface, the payload expands into the following character stream:

```json
{
  "call_id": "call_98124_x",
  "tool_name": "write_file",
  "arguments": {
    "path": "src/auth/jwt.py",
    "content": "def decode_token(token: str) -> dict:\n    return jwt.decode(token, secret, algorithms=[\"HS256\"])\n"
  }
}
```

To quantify this overhead, @tbl-token-compression-ratios compares the raw payload byte size against the token consumption across different operational tool payloads when encoded using the standard `o200k_base` tokenizer.

| Workload / Action Description | Raw Payload Size (Bytes) | Token Count (Direct Text) | Token Count (JSON Tool Call) | Serialization Tax (Token Inflation) | Compression Ratio (Bytes / Token) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Shell Command Execution** (`git diff --stat HEAD~1`) | 27 B | 6 tokens | 22 tokens | **+266.6%** | 1.22 B/token |
| **Python File Modification** (35-line auth function) | 1,142 B | 278 tokens | 412 tokens | **+48.2%** | 2.77 B/token |
| **AST JSON Schema Definition** (Tool parameter specs) | 856 B | 164 tokens | 258 tokens | **+57.3%** | 3.31 B/token |
| **SQL Database Query** (Multi-table join with filters) | 184 B | 38 tokens | 74 tokens | **+94.7%** | 2.48 B/token |

: Empirical measurement of the serialization tax across standard agentic tool-invocation payloads (measured against the `o200k_base` vocabulary). {#tbl-token-compression-ratios}

As demonstrated in @tbl-token-compression-ratios, short tool invocations (such as shell commands) suffer a token inflation penalty exceeding $200\%$ due to fixed structural overhead. For long code patches, the serialization tax stabilizes near $50\%$. In a long-horizon agent trajectory involving dozens of tool-invocation turns, thousands of tokens—and their associated memory allocation in the serving engine—are expended purely transmitting JSON formatting trivia.

### Sequence Length Constraints, Truncation Hazards, and the Quarantining Invariant

Every model invocation is bounded by a hard physical context ceiling. Let $M$ represent the number of staged input prompt tokens, and let $K$ represent the number of candidate tokens generated during the decode phase. The total sequence length $S$ is strictly governed by the maximum sequence capacity $S_{\max}$ supported by the model's architectural positional encodings and the memory budget of the serving runtime:

$$S = M + K \le S_{\max}$$ {#eq-sequence-ceiling}

When the host runtime issues an inference request, it specifies an explicit decode ceiling $K_{\max}$ representing the maximum number of tokens the engine is permitted to emit for that invocation turn ($K \le K_{\max}$). This parameter prevents the model from entering an unbounded autoregressive generation loop that exhausts budget or monopolizes accelerator compute.

This constraint introduces a severe operational hazard: the **Truncation Hazard**. If the generation phase exhausts its allocation ($k = K_{\max}$) or if the sequence reaches the context ceiling ($M + k = S_{\max}$) before the model emits an explicit end-of-sequence token (`<|eot_id|>`, `</s>`, or an engine-level stop sequence), the serving engine abruptly halts generation.

When generation halts due to sequence exhaustion, the emitted string is incomplete. In the context of structured tool calls, truncation produces syntactically mangled payloads:

```json
{"name": "execute_bash", "arguments": {"command": "rm -rf /tmp/scratch_build_
```

If an undisciplined agent runtime attempts to parse this incomplete emission, standard JSON parsers fail with an unexpected EOF syntax error (`json.decoder.JSONDecodeError`). Worse, if an agent utilizes a relaxed, streaming, or error-tolerant parser that attempts to "repair" broken JSON by auto-closing open quotation marks and brackets, the resulting execution payload may be catastrophic:

$$\text{Repaired Payload: } \texttt{\{"command": "rm -rf /tmp/scratch\_build\_"\}}$$

If the original intent of the model was to emit `rm -rf /tmp/scratch_build_dir/output.log` and replace it with fresh data, executing a truncated command string risks deleting unintended system paths or hanging child processes.

To prevent this class of failure, robust agent operating systems enforce **The Quarantining Invariant**:

::: {.callout-important title="The Invariant: The Quarantining Invariant"}
Any candidate sequence emitted under a non-clean stop condition (e.g., `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` or `stop_reason == "length"`) must be treated as structurally corrupt and strictly quarantined within host memory escrow. Under the zero ambient authority principle ($A=0$), truncated emissions must never be forwarded to downstream parser-repair heuristics or dispatched to host tool effectors.
:::

When a truncation condition is detected via the inference status envelope, the host supervisor rejects the candidate output in its entirety. The supervisor logs the generation boundary violation to the state ledger and either prompts the model with an explicit continuation exception or truncates prior context history to afford a larger generation budget $K_{\max}$.

Having established how raw byte streams are translated into discrete tokens, gathered into dense vector matrices within accelerator memory, and bounded by context-length limits, we must now examine how the inference engine processes these vectors. Transforming staged input tokens into candidate completions is not a static one-pass compilation; it requires an iterative, step-by-step execution loop that repeatedly queries the neural network to produce one token at a time.

## Autoregressive Generation and the Serving Loop {#sec-vol3-processor-autoregressive}

At the foundation of autoregressive sequence generation lies an irreducibly serial computational graph. Unlike classical batch compilers that translate an entire source module in a single structured sweep, a generative neural language model cannot evaluate its complete output sequence in parallel. Because each successive token's probability distribution is strictly conditioned on the sequence of tokens that precede it, generating an output sequence of length $K$ mandates an iterative serving loop that evaluates the deep neural network $K$ successive times. Each evaluation constitutes an atomic forward pass across accelerator silicon, computing an unnormalized probability distribution over the discrete vocabulary, sampling a single token, and appending that token to the sequence buffer before initiating the next physical cycle.

### Autoregressive Factorization and the Causal Dependency Chain

The mathematical formulation of sequence generation governs this serial execution pipeline. Let $x = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_M)$ denote the staged input prompt comprising $M$ discrete tokens, and let $y = (y_1, y_2, \dots, y_K)$ denote the candidate output sequence comprising $K$ discrete tokens. The joint probability of the complete sequence $y$ conditioned on the input prompt $x$ is factorized via the chain rule of probability into a product of conditional distributions:

$$P(y_{1:K} \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^{K} P(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})$$ {#eq-autoregressive-factorization}

where $y_{<t} = (y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})$ represents the sequence of candidate tokens generated prior to step $t$, with $y_{<1} = \emptyset$. Equation @eq-autoregressive-factorization establishes the fundamental architectural invariant of the autoregressive serving loop: the conditional probability distribution at step $t$ cannot be computed in isolation because its conditioning context requires the concrete realization of all preceding tokens $y_1$ through $y_{t-1}$.

In classical superscalar microprocessor architectures, hardware pipelines actively exploit instruction-level parallelism (ILP) through dynamic out-of-order scheduling, register renaming, and speculative branch execution. When an out-of-order execution engine detects that instruction $B$ does not share a true data dependency with instruction $A$, it dispatches both instructions to parallel execution units simultaneously. Even when evaluating conditional branches, hardware branch predictors evaluate speculative execution paths dozens of instructions ahead of program order, committing architectural state only when the branch condition is resolved.

Autoregressive token generation precludes this class of speculative bypass along a single trajectory. In an agentic execution system, the generation of token $y_t$ exhibits a true data dependency of the most unyielding variety: the discrete identity of token $y_{t-1}$ determines the exact embedding row gathered into the input layer of the neural network at step $t$. Furthermore, because token selection is non-deterministic—governed by a parameterized probability distribution sampled over a vocabulary simplex of tens or hundreds of thousands of candidates—the serving daemon cannot resolve which token will be appended at step $t$ until step $t-1$ has fully traversed all transformer layers, projected its final activations into vocabulary space, and executed the host sampling policy. No speculative pipeline can evaluate step $t+1$ before step $t$ has materialized. The generation trajectory is fundamentally, physically serialized.

### The Decode Execution Cycle and Vocabulary Projection

The mechanical execution of autoregressive generation is orchestrated by an iterative serving loop within the inference runtime. Each cycle of this loop executes a deterministic sequence of operations across the host supervisor and the neural accelerator, as illustrated in @fig-autoregressive-serving-loop.

::: {#fig-autoregressive-serving-loop}
```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           THE AUTOREGRESSIVE SERVING LOOP                     |
|                                                                               |
|   +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 1. Context Staging: Sequence Buffer s_t = [x_1, ..., x_M, y_1, ..., y_{t-1}] |
|   +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+   |
|                                       |
|                                       v Dispatch Forward Pass
|   +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 2. Deep Transformer Stack: Multi-Head Attention & Feed-Forward MLPs   |   |
|   |    Emits final-position hidden representation: h_t in R^{d_model}     |   |
|   +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+   |
|                                       |
|                                       v Linear Unembedding Projection
|   +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 3. Vocabulary Unembedding: z_t = W_unembed * h_t  (z_t in R^{|V|})    |   |
|   +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+   |
|                                       |
|                                       v Logit Normalization (Softmax & Temp)
|   +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 4. Distribution Shaping: P_tau(y_t | s_t) = Softmax(z_t / tau)        |   |
|   |    Apply Top-k / Top-p Truncation Filters                             |   |
|   +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+   |
|                                       |
|                                       v Pseudo-Random Uniform Sample
|   +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 5. Token Sampling: Select discrete token index y_t in V               |   |
|   +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+   |
|                                       |
|             +-------------------------+-------------------------+
|             | Check Stop Conditions                             |
|             v                                                   v
|   [Match EOS or Stop Delimiter]                       [Continue Generation]
|   Terminate: Status = COMPLETED                       Append y_t to s_{t+1}
|   Forward candidate to Host Escrow                    Loop to Step 1 (t <- t+1)
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The Autoregressive Decode Serving Loop. Each cycle computes an atomic forward pass for the latest position, projects hidden activations into vocabulary logits, shapes the resulting probability distribution, samples a discrete token, and checks termination invariants.
:::

Let $\mathbf{s}_t = [x_1, \dots, x_M, y_1, \dots, y_{t-1}]$ represent the complete token sequence presented to the inference engine at iteration $t$. The execution cycle proceeds through five distinct stages:

1. **Forward Pass Evaluation:** The accelerator evaluates the deep transformer layers for the newest sequence position. The network propagates activations through stacked layers of multi-head self-attention and non-linear feed-forward sublayers, ultimately yielding a dense hidden activation vector for the terminal position:
$$\mathbf{h}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$$
where $d_{\text{model}}$ denotes the hidden dimension of the transformer (typically ranging from $4{,}096$ to $12{,}288$ in modern production foundation models).

2. **Vocabulary Unembedding Projection:** The hidden activation $\mathbf{h}_t$ is projected across the entire discrete vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ via the unembedding matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\text{unembed}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d_{\text{model}}}$:
$$\mathbf{z}_t = \mathbf{W}_{\text{unembed}} \, \mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}_{\text{unembed}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$$
The resulting vector $\mathbf{z}_t$ consists of raw, unnormalized real-valued logits. Each entry $z_{t, v}$ corresponds to a discrete subword token $v \in \mathcal{V}$. In large vocabulary models (such as modern tokenizers with $|\mathcal{V}| \approx 128{,}000$ to $256{,}000$), this projection alone requires computing hundreds of thousands of inner products per token generated.

3. **Probability Normalization:** To convert unbounded logits into a valid probability distribution lying on the probability simplex $\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|-1}$, the serving daemon computes the softmax function over the logit vector:
$$P(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{s}_t) = \frac{\exp(z_{t, v})}{\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|} \exp(z_{t, j})}$$ {#eq-standard-softmax}
where $P(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{s}_t) \ge 0$ and $\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} P(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{s}_t) = 1$.

4. **Stochastic Token Sampling:** The serving runtime draws a pseudo-random scalar $u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and inverts the cumulative distribution function over $\mathcal{V}$ to select a discrete token identifier $y_t$.

5. **Sequence Mutation and Invariant Checking:** The sampled token index $y_t$ is appended to the sequence buffer, producing the expanded context $\mathbf{s}_{t+1} = [\mathbf{s}_t, y_t]$. The serving engine verifies termination invariants against predefined stopping criteria. If no termination boundary is encountered and $t < K_{\max}$, the loop increments $t \leftarrow t + 1$ and dispatches the subsequent accelerator execution.

### Probability Shaping: Temperature Scaling and Simplex Truncation

The raw softmax transformation in Equation @eq-standard-softmax treats model logits directly as log-odds. In practical agent systems, the host runtime must control the dispersion of entropy across the vocabulary simplex to modulate generation determinism. This control is governed primarily by **temperature scaling** ($\tau$).

Let $\tau \in (0, \infty)$ denote a strictly positive real-valued hyperparameter. The temperature-scaled probability distribution is defined as:

$$P_\tau(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{s}_t) = \frac{\exp\left(\frac{z_{t, v}}{\tau}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|} \exp\left(\frac{z_{t, j}}{\tau}\right)}$$ {#eq-temperature-softmax}

The temperature scalar acts as an inverse thermodynamic energy parameter across the vocabulary distribution:

- **Greedy Argmax Limit ($\tau \to 0^+$):** As $\tau$ approaches zero, the ratio between the largest logit and all competing logits approaches infinity. The exponentiated mass concentrates entirely on the single token possessing the maximum logit value:
$$\lim_{\tau \to 0^+} P_\tau(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{s}_t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } v = \arg\max_{j \in \mathcal{V}} z_{t, j} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Greedy decoding renders the serving loop completely deterministic for a given input sequence and model checkpoint. In software engineering agents tasked with structured schema generation or tool calling, low temperatures ($\tau \le 0.2$) or greedy decoding are frequently mandated to minimize syntax errors and ensure reproducible code output.
- **Calibrated Training Density ($\tau = 1.0$):** At unit temperature, the probabilities reflect the unscaled training likelihood distribution.
- **Maximum Entropy Dispersion ($\tau \to \infty$):** As $\tau$ grows large, the scaled logits $z_{t, v} / \tau$ converge toward zero. Consequently, $\exp(0) = 1$ for all vocabulary entries, causing the distribution to degenerate into a uniform distribution:
$$\lim_{\tau \to \infty} P_\tau(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{s}_t) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}$$
Under elevated temperatures, the sampler draws from low-probability tokens, causing the generated text to lose grammatical cohesion.

To prevent the sampler from drawing improbable tokens from the long tail of the vocabulary distribution—an occurrence that frequently introduces syntax corruptions or invalid subwords into structured payloads—production inference runtimes apply truncation filters prior to sampling:

- **Top-$k$ Truncation:** The engine restricts the candidate set to the $k$ tokens possessing the highest logit values. Let $\mathcal{V}_k \subset \mathcal{V}$ denote this top-$k$ subset, where $|\mathcal{V}_k| = k$. The logits of all tokens outside $\mathcal{V}_k$ are set to $-\infty$:
$$z'_{t, v} = \begin{cases} z_{t, v} & \text{if } v \in \mathcal{V}_k \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
- **Top-$p$ (Nucleus) Truncation:** Fixed $k$ filtering suffers from a structural flaw: when the model is highly confident, $k$ tokens may include many implausible candidates; conversely, when the distribution is flat, $k$ tokens may exclude valid possibilities. Nucleus sampling dynamically sizes the candidate set by selecting the smallest subset of tokens $\mathcal{V}_p \subset \mathcal{V}$ whose cumulative probability mass meets or exceeds a predefined threshold $p \in (0, 1]$:
$$\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_p} P_\tau(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{s}_t) \ge p$$
Logits for tokens outside $\mathcal{V}_p$ are set to $-\infty$, and the remaining distribution is renormalized. This dynamically contracts the candidate pool during unambiguous syntax transitions and expands it when multiple valid continuations exist.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Temperature Scaling on the Vocabulary Simplex"}
To observe the quantitative impact of temperature scaling on vocabulary selection, consider a concrete systems scenario where a model's unembedding layer emits raw logits over a miniature three-token vocabulary:
$$\mathcal{V} = \{v_1: \texttt{"def"}, \; v_2: \texttt{"class"}, \; v_3: \texttt{"import"}\}$$
Suppose the forward pass produces the raw logit vector:
$$\mathbf{z} = [6.0, \; 4.0, \; 2.0]$$
We compute the resulting probability distribution across three distinct operational regimes: unit temperature ($\tau = 1.0$), low temperature ($\tau = 0.5$), and high temperature ($\tau = 2.0$).

**Step 1: Standard Evaluation ($\tau = 1.0$):**
We compute the exponentiated logits:
$$\exp(6.0) \approx 403.43, \quad \exp(4.0) \approx 54.60, \quad \exp(2.0) \approx 7.39$$
The normalization denominator is:
$$\sum_{j=1}^3 \exp(z_j) = 403.43 + 54.60 + 7.39 = 465.42$$
The resulting probabilities are:
$$P(v_1) = \frac{403.43}{465.42} \approx 86.68\%, \quad P(v_2) = \frac{54.60}{465.42} \approx 11.73\%, \quad P(v_3) = \frac{7.39}{465.42} \approx 1.59\%$$

**Step 2: Low-Temperature Sharpening ($\tau = 0.5$):**
Scaling the logits by $\tau = 0.5$ yields $\mathbf{z} / 0.5 = [12.0, \; 8.0, \; 4.0]$. Exponentiating yields:
$$\exp(12.0) \approx 162{,}754.79, \quad \exp(8.0) \approx 2{,}980.96, \quad \exp(4.0) \approx 54.60$$
The normalization denominator is:
$$\sum_{j=1}^3 \exp\left(\frac{z_j}{0.5}\right) = 162{,}754.79 + 2{,}980.96 + 54.60 = 165{,}790.35$$
The resulting probabilities are:
$$P(v_1) \approx 98.17\%, \quad P(v_2) \approx 1.80\%, \quad P(v_3) \approx 0.03\%$$
Under $\tau = 0.5$, the probability of selecting the dominant token $v_1$ increases from $86.68\%$ to $98.17\%$, while the probability of $v_3$ drops by more than a factor of 50.

**Step 3: High-Temperature Flattening ($\tau = 2.0$):**
Scaling the logits by $\tau = 2.0$ yields $\mathbf{z} / 2.0 = [3.0, \; 2.0, \; 1.0]$. Exponentiating yields:
$$\exp(3.0) \approx 20.09, \quad \exp(2.0) \approx 7.39, \quad \exp(1.0) \approx 2.72$$
The normalization denominator is:
$$\sum_{j=1}^3 \exp\left(\frac{z_j}{2.0}\right) = 20.09 + 7.39 + 2.72 = 30.20$$
The resulting probabilities are:
$$P(v_1) \approx 66.52\%, \quad P(v_2) \approx 24.47\%, \quad P(v_3) \approx 9.01\%$$

| Candidate Token | Raw Logit $z$ | $P(\tau = 1.0)$ | $P(\tau = 0.5)$ | $P(\tau = 2.0)$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $v_1 = \texttt{"def"}$ | $6.0$ | $86.68\%$ | $98.17\%$ | $66.52\%$ |
| $v_2 = \texttt{"class"}$ | $4.0$ | $11.73\%$ | $1.80\%$ | $24.47\%$ |
| $v_3 = \texttt{"import"}$ | $2.0$ | $1.59\%$ | $0.03\%$ | $9.01\%$ |

*Takeaway:* Reducing temperature concentrates probability mass aggressively onto the highest-scoring candidate, suppressing tail entropy and enforcing structural consistency. Elevating temperature disperses probability mass across competing candidates, elevating non-deterministic variation at the expense of syntactic fidelity.
:::

### Termination Mechanics and Stop Condition Monitoring

The serving loop cannot execute indefinitely; it requires formal termination invariants to break its serial iteration and return control to the host supervisor. In production inference systems, termination is triggered by three distinct mechanical conditions:

1. **Native End-of-Sequence (`EOS`) Detection:** Foundation models are trained with special control tokens designating sequence completion (such as `<|endoftext|>`, `</s>`, or `<|eot_id|>`). When the stochastic sampling routine selects the vocabulary ID corresponding to the model's native `EOS` token, the inference engine halts the decode loop immediately. The output status is marked as `COMPLETED`.

2. **Multi-Token Stop Delimiters:** In agent systems, tool invocations, code blocks, or structured outputs often conclude with domain-specific string markers rather than global `EOS` tokens. For example, an agent runtime may configure the inference engine to halt upon generating the closing markdown delimiter ```` or a structured XML tag such as `</tool_call>`. Monitoring for custom stop delimiters introduces a subtle systems challenge: subword fragmentation. Because a stop delimiter (such as `</tool_call>`) may be decomposed into multiple subword tokens (such as `["</", "tool", "_call", ">"]`), the serving engine cannot simply match individual token IDs. Instead, it maintains a sliding character buffer over recent emissions. When candidate tokens form a partial prefix of a stop sequence, the engine buffers those tokens, withholding them from client-facing streaming interfaces until subsequent tokens either complete the delimiter match or diverge. When a complete match occurs, the serving engine strips the delimiter characters from the candidate payload and marks the invocation status as `COMPLETED`.

3. **Decode Token Ceilings ($K_{\max}$):** To prevent infinite generation loops resulting from model degradation or repetitive cycles, the host supervisor enforces a strict generation budget $K_{\max}$. If the decode counter reaches $t = K_{\max}$ without encountering an `EOS` token or stop delimiter, the serving runtime forcefully aborts the generation loop. In accordance with strict systems contracts, the engine marks the response with the status `TRUNCATED`.

To ensure safe inter-process communication, the serving engine packages the output into a normalized status envelope. As established under the zero ambient authority principle ($A=0$), the supervisor must strictly discriminate between the four canonical invocation outcomes:
- `COMPLETED`: The model concluded generation cleanly via an `EOS` token or an explicit stop delimiter. The payload in escrow is structurally intact.
- `TRUNCATED`: Generation was forcibly severed due to context ceiling exhaustion ($S \ge S_{\max}$) or decode budget expiration ($t \ge K_{\max}$). Under the Quarantining Invariant, this payload is treated as structurally corrupt and quarantined.
- `REFUSED`: The model's safety alignment mechanisms intervened to suppress output generation.
- `TRANSPORT_FAILURE`: The underlying network connection was severed, a socket timed out, or the accelerator runtime crashed.

The mechanics of the autoregressive serving loop expose an extreme operational dichotomy across accelerator hardware. When processing the initial staged prompt of $M$ tokens, the neural network can ingest and transform the entire sequence in parallel using high-density matrix multiplication kernels. Once generation transitions to the decode phase, however, this parallelism collapses entirely: every single token generated requires a distinct forward pass that must shuttle tens of billions of model parameters across the accelerator memory bus simply to produce a single vector of logits. To understand why single-batch agent trajectories incur substantial latency and how physical memory bandwidth dictates operational costs, we must transition from the algorithmic logic of the serving loop to the underlying accelerator hardware physics governing prompt prefill and token decode.

## Prefill, Decode, and Accelerator Hardware Physics {#sec-vol3-processor-cost}

An accelerator executing a foundation model does not operate in a single, uniform execution regime; it bifurcates into two computational phases governed by fundamentally different physical limits. When processing the initial staged prompt of $M$ tokens, the accelerator functions as a massively parallel compute engine running matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM) that saturate hardware floating-point units. The instant generation transitions to producing output tokens, this parallel efficiency collapses: the accelerator is forced into an iterative sequence of matrix-vector multiplications (GEMV) where execution speed is constrained by the speed of reading model parameters from High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM).

Understanding this split is essential for systems engineers. In single-trajectory agentic workloads, the host runtime cannot arbitrarily scale batch sizes to mask latency. To optimize agent responsiveness, manage timeouts, and budget token allocations, we must ground our software architectures in the physical realities of memory bandwidth, operational intensity, and accelerator hardware limits.

### The Roofline Model and the Dual-Regime Nature of Inference

The performance boundary of any accelerator kernel is governed by Williams, Waterman, and Patterson's **Roofline Model** [-@williams2009roofline]. The model relates the achievable computational performance $P$ (measured in floating-point operations per second, $\text{FLOP/s}$) to the processor's peak theoretical compute throughput $P_{\text{peak}}$ and its memory bandwidth $\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}$ (bytes per second) through a fundamental metric known as **arithmetic intensity** (or operational intensity), denoted by $I$:

$$I = \frac{\text{Total Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs)}}{\text{Total Memory Traffic (Bytes Transferred)}} \quad \left[\frac{\text{FLOP}}{\text{byte}}\right]$$

The attainable performance of a given workload is bounded by the minimum of the hardware's compute ceiling and the product of its memory bandwidth with the kernel's arithmetic intensity:

$$P = \min\left(P_{\text{peak}}, \; \text{BW}_{\text{mem}} \times I\right)$$

The intersection of these two asymptotes defines the hardware's **saturation arithmetic intensity**, $I_{\text{sat}}$:

$$I_{\text{sat}} = \frac{P_{\text{peak}}}{\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}} \quad \left[\frac{\text{FLOP}}{\text{byte}}\right]$$

When an algorithm's arithmetic intensity $I \ge I_{\text{sat}}$, execution is **compute-bound**; the arithmetic units (such as GPU Tensor Cores) are fully saturated, and memory bandwidth is not the limiting factor. Conversely, when $I < I_{\text{sat}}$, execution is **memory-bandwidth-bound**; compute units sit idle waiting for operands to arrive from off-chip dynamic RAM or HBM.

```
       Attainable Performance P [TFLOP/s]
             ▲
P_peak ──────┼─────────────────────────╭──────────────────────── (Compute Ceiling)
(989 TFLOP/s)│                        /│
             │                       / │  Compute-Bound Regime
             │                      /  │  (Prefill GEMM: I >> I_sat)
             │                     /   │
             │                    /    │
             │                   /     │
             │                  /      │
             │                 /       │
             │  Memory-Bound  /        │
             │  Regime       /         │
             │  (Decode     /          │
             │   GEMV:     /           │
             │   I ~ 1)   /            │
             │           /             │
             └──────────┴──────────────┴───────────────────────►
                       1.0           295.2 (I_sat)        Arithmetic Intensity I
                                                          [FLOP/byte]
```

To ground this in production hardware, consider the datacenter-standard NVIDIA H100 SXM5 accelerator:
- **Peak Dense Compute ($P_{\text{peak}}$):** $989 \times 10^{12} \text{ FLOP/s}$ ($989\text{ TFLOP/s}$) in dense 16-bit floating-point (FP16/BF16) Tensor Core operations.
- **Memory Bandwidth ($\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}$):** $3.35 \times 10^{12} \text{ bytes/s}$ ($3.35\text{ TB/s}$) across an 80 GiB HBM3 bus.

Applying the saturation formulation:

$$I_{\text{sat}} = \frac{989 \times 10^{12}\text{ FLOP/s}}{3.35 \times 10^{12}\text{ bytes/s}} \approx 295.2\text{ FLOP/byte}$$

To run the H100's Tensor Cores at $100\%$ utilization, a computational kernel must execute at least $295.2$ floating-point calculations for every single byte loaded across the HBM bus.

A transformer inference invocation traverses two computational phases with radically different arithmetic intensities:

#### 1. The Prefill Phase (Prompt Processing)

During prefill, the serving runtime ingests all $M$ staged tokens of the prompt simultaneously. For a linear layer with weight matrix $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$, the activations of the $M$ tokens are grouped into a dense input matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times M}$. Computing the layer output:

$$\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times M}$$

This operation is a dense General Matrix-Matrix Multiplication (GEMM). Evaluating $\mathbf{Y}$ requires $2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot d_{\text{in}} \cdot M$ floating-point operations (each matrix multiply-accumulate represents one multiplication and one addition, or $2\text{ FLOPs}$).

Assuming weights are loaded once from HBM into on-chip SRAM, reading $\mathbf{W}$ in FP16 ($2\text{ bytes/parameter}$) transfers $2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot d_{\text{in}}$ bytes. Reading $\mathbf{X}$ transfers $2 \cdot d_{\text{in}} \cdot M$ bytes, and writing $\mathbf{Y}$ transfers $2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot M$ bytes. For substantial prompt lengths ($M \gg 1$), the parameter weight matrix dominates the memory transfer overhead:

$$I_{\text{prefill}} \approx \frac{2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot d_{\text{in}} \cdot M\text{ FLOPs}}{2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot d_{\text{in}}\text{ bytes}} = M\text{ FLOP/byte}$$

Because the weights loaded from HBM are reused $M$ times across all prompt token activations in on-chip caches, the arithmetic intensity scales linearly with prompt length $M$. For an agent prompt containing $M = 4{,}000$ tokens:

$$I_{\text{prefill}} \approx 4{,}000\text{ FLOP/byte} \gg I_{\text{sat}} \; (295.2\text{ FLOP/byte})$$

The prefill phase operates deeply within the **compute-bound regime**. Tensor Cores are driven to near-maximum utilization, making prefill throughput depend directly on the accelerator's peak raw compute throughput ($P_{\text{peak}}$). This phase determines the **Time-to-First-Token (TTFT)**.

#### 2. The Decode Phase (Autoregressive Generation)

Once the prompt is ingested, autoregressive generation produces one token at a time. To generate token $t+1$, the model cannot execute a GEMM because the future activation does not yet exist. Instead, the model evaluates a single activation vector $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times 1}$ against the weight matrix $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$:

$$\mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times 1}$$

This operation is a General Matrix-Vector Multiplication (GEMV). Evaluating $\mathbf{y}_t$ requires $2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot d_{\text{in}}$ FLOPs. However, to execute this single vector transformation, the accelerator must read the entire weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$ from HBM:

$$I_{\text{decode}} = \frac{2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot d_{\text{in}}\text{ FLOPs}}{2 \cdot d_{\text{out}} \cdot d_{\text{in}}\text{ bytes (weights)} + 2(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\text{ bytes (activations)}} \approx 1.0\text{ FLOP/byte}$$

At an arithmetic intensity of $I_{\text{decode}} \approx 1.0\text{ FLOP/byte}$, the H100 SXM5 operates far below its saturation threshold ($I_{\text{sat}} = 295.2$). The achievable compute throughput during unbatched decode is strictly limited by memory bandwidth:

$$P_{\text{decode}} = \text{BW}_{\text{mem}} \times I_{\text{decode}} = 3.35 \times 10^{12} \text{ bytes/s} \times 1.0 \text{ FLOP/byte} = 3.35\text{ TFLOP/s}$$

Dividing this by the hardware ceiling demonstrates the stark hardware inefficiency of single-sequence autoregression:

$$\text{Utilization} = \frac{P_{\text{decode}}}{P_{\text{peak}}} = \frac{3.35\text{ TFLOP/s}}{989\text{ TFLOP/s}} \approx 0.00339 \implies \mathbf{0.34\%}$$

During unbatched token generation, **over 99.6% of the accelerator's Tensor Core compute capacity sits completely idle**. The processor is reduced to a memory-streaming pipeline. We can think of the GPU as a high-performance sports car engine fed by a narrow cocktail straw: the engine can consume massive amounts of fuel, but the rate of fuel flowing through the straw throttles system performance. In decode mode, the width of the straw—HBM interface bandwidth—dictates output speed.

---

### The HBM Parameter Shuttle Floor and Decode Physics

Because decode arithmetic intensity is clamped near unity, generating each individual token requires streaming the active parameters of the foundation model across the accelerator's memory bus from HBM into on-chip register files and SRAM caches. This physical data movement establishes an inviolable lower bound on per-token generation latency: the **HBM Parameter Shuttle Floor**.

Let $P_{\text{params}}$ represent the active parameter count of the model architecture, and let $b_{\text{weight}}$ denote the precision representation in bytes per parameter ($b_{\text{weight}} = 2$ for FP16/BF16, $b_{\text{weight}} = 1$ for FP8, and $b_{\text{weight}} = 0.5$ for INT4). The total weight payload $Q_{\text{weights}}$ transferred across the memory bus for a single decode step is:

$$Q_{\text{weights}} = P_{\text{params}} \cdot b_{\text{weight}} \quad [\text{bytes}]$$

The theoretical minimum time to transfer these weights across an accelerator memory bus with effective sustained bandwidth $\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}$ yields the fundamental per-token latency floor:

$$T_{\text{decode, token}} \ge \frac{Q_{\text{weights}}}{\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}} = \frac{P_{\text{params}} \cdot b_{\text{weight}}}{\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}} \quad [\text{seconds/token}]$$

Taking the reciprocal yields the maximum theoretical decode throughput for an unbatched request ($B = 1$):

$$\text{Throughput}_{\max} \le \frac{\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}}{P_{\text{params}} \cdot b_{\text{weight}}} \quad [\text{tokens/second}]$$

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Sizing the HBM Parameter Shuttle Floor"}
Consider an autonomous coding agent executing against an open-weights 70-billion parameter model ($P_{\text{params}} = 70 \times 10^9$) deployed on an NVIDIA H100 SXM5 accelerator with $80\text{ GiB}$ of HBM3 and an interface bandwidth of $\text{BW}_{\text{mem}} = 3.35\text{ TB/s}$ ($3.35 \times 10^{12}\text{ bytes/s}$).

**Case A: 16-Bit Floating Point (FP16 / BF16)**
At 16-bit precision, each parameter occupies $b_{\text{weight}} = 2\text{ bytes}$.
The total memory volume that must be shuttled across the bus per token is:
$$Q_{\text{weights}} = 70 \times 10^9 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 140 \times 10^9\text{ bytes} = 140\text{ GB}$$

*(Note: Storing a 140 GB model requires pooling memory across multiple physical accelerators; here we evaluate the bandwidth floor across the aggregate memory bus).*

The absolute physical latency floor to emit a single token is:
$$T_{\text{decode, token}} \ge \frac{140 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}}{3.35 \times 10^{12}\text{ bytes/s}} \approx 0.04179\text{ seconds} \approx \mathbf{41.8\text{ ms/token}}$$

The maximum theoretical generation throughput is:
$$\text{Throughput}_{\max} \le \frac{1}{0.04179\text{ s}} \approx \mathbf{23.9\text{ tokens/second}}$$

**Case B: 8-Bit Quantized Float (FP8)**
If the model weights are quantized to FP8 ($b_{\text{weight}} = 1\text{ byte}$), the memory shuttle payload drops by half:
$$Q_{\text{weights}} = 70 \times 10^9 \times 1\text{ byte} = 70\text{ GB}$$

The latency floor drops proportionally:
$$T_{\text{decode, token}} \ge \frac{70 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}}{3.35 \times 10^{12}\text{ bytes/s}} \approx 0.02090\text{ seconds} \approx \mathbf{20.9\text{ ms/token}}$$

Yielding a maximum unbatched throughput ceiling of:
$$\text{Throughput}_{\max} \le \frac{1}{0.02090\text{ s}} \approx \mathbf{47.8\text{ tokens/second}}$$

No compiler optimization, CUDA kernel fusion, or architectural framework can overcome this physical limit. If an engineer expects an unbatched 70B parameter model in FP16 to generate $100\text{ tokens/s}$ on this hardware, their expectation contradicts the laws of memory bus physics.
:::

In practice, the true per-token decode latency is slightly higher than this parameter floor. In addition to reading the model weights $Q_{\text{weights}}$, the accelerator must also read the historical Key and Value cache activations for all preceding tokens in the context window to evaluate multi-head attention. For a sequence of length $S$, this requires transferring additional memory:

$$Q_{\text{KV}}(S) = 2 \cdot L \cdot H_{\text{KV}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot S \cdot b_{\text{KV}} \quad [\text{bytes}]$$

Where $L$ is the number of transformer layers, $H_{\text{KV}}$ is the number of key-value attention heads, $d_{\text{head}}$ is head dimension, and $b_{\text{KV}}$ is cache precision. While $Q_{\text{weights}}$ remains constant across generation, $Q_{\text{KV}}(S)$ grows monotonically as generation extends, compounding memory bus congestion at large context depths.

To capture and monitor these constraints within an agent host runtime, systems maintain precise latency profiles that decouple memory transfer constraints from host execution overhead. The Python dataclass in @lst-latency-profile illustrates how production runtimes track these metrics across model invocations.

```python
# Listing 2.1: Python dataclass modeling invocation latency decomposition.
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class InvocationLatencyProfile:
    """Profiles the hardware and software latency components of a model call."""
    # Token Counts
    prompt_tokens: int            # M: Tokens processed in prefill GEMM
    completion_tokens: int        # K: Tokens generated in decode GEMV

    # Software & Queue Overhead (Host CPU)
    t_prep_ms: float              # Tokenization, prompt formatting, context assembly
    t_queue_ms: float             # Time spent waiting in the serving engine queue

    # Hardware Execution Breakdown (Accelerator)
    t_ttft_ms: float              # Time-to-First-Token: t_prep + t_queue + t_prefill
    t_prefill_ms: float           # Pure accelerator GEMM prefill computation
    t_decode_total_ms: float      # Cumulative time across all K decode cycles

    # Derived Physical Hardware Metrics
    sustained_hbm_bandwidth_tbs: float  # Measured sustained HBM bandwidth
    active_param_count: float           # Model parameter count (e.g., 70e9)
    weight_precision_bytes: float       # Bytes per weight parameter (e.g., 1.0 for FP8)

    @property
    def inter_token_latency_ms(self) -> float:
        """Mean Inter-Token Latency (ITL) during the decode phase."""
        if self.completion_tokens <= 1:
            return 0.0
        return self.t_decode_total_ms / (self.completion_tokens - 1)

    @property
    def physical_shuttle_floor_ms(self) -> float:
        """Physical HBM weight shuttle floor per token (ms)."""
        bytes_per_token = self.active_param_count * self.weight_precision_bytes
        bw_bytes_per_sec = self.sustained_hbm_bandwidth_tbs * 1e12
        return (bytes_per_token / bw_bytes_per_sec) * 1000.0

    @property
    def bus_efficiency(self) -> float:
        """Ratio of theoretical physical shuttle minimum to actual ITL."""
        if self.inter_token_latency_ms == 0.0:
            return 1.0
        return min(1.0, self.physical_shuttle_floor_ms / self.inter_token_latency_ms)
```

---

### Workload Asymmetry, Latency Decomposition, and the Batching Dilemma

Understanding the distinct physics of prefill and decode clarifies a fundamental architectural divergence: **agentic workloads exhibit a radical workload asymmetry compared to standard conversational applications**.

In typical conversational chatbot applications, input prompts and output responses are roughly symmetric in token volume: a user submits a prompt of $M \approx 500$ tokens and receives an explanatory response of $K \approx 500$ tokens. In this setting, the overall request latency is heavily dominated by the decode phase. At $25\text{ ms/token}$, generating $500$ tokens consumes $12.5\text{ seconds}$, whereas the initial prefill consumes less than $100\text{ ms}$.

Autonomous software engineering agents (such as Claude Code, Devin, or SWE-agent) invert this profile completely. A production coding agent must ingest comprehensive repository maps, abstract syntax trees, documentation context, multi-file source listings, and lengthy execution logs from failing test suites. Consequently, the staged prompt length $M$ regularly scales to tens of thousands of tokens ($M \ge 40{,}000$). Conversely, when the agent decides its next action, it emits a concise, structured tool invocation—such as writing a shell command, requesting a file edit, or issuing a patch. These structured payloads are brief, typically requiring $K \approx 50\text{ to }150$ tokens.

| Architectural Dimension | Conversational Chatbot | Autonomous Software Agent |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Typical Prompt Length ($M$)** | $200 - 1{,}000\text{ tokens}$ | $20{,}000 - 100{,}000\text{ tokens}$ |
| **Typical Generation Length ($K$)** | $300 - 1{,}000\text{ tokens}$ | $40 - 200\text{ tokens}$ (Tool Invocation) |
| **Token Ratio ($M : K$)** | $\approx 1 : 1$ | $\approx \mathbf{200 : 1}\text{ to }\mathbf{1{,}000 : 1}$ |
| **Primary Latency Bottleneck** | Decode Phase (Inter-Token Latency) | Prefill Phase (Time-to-First-Token) |
| **Accelerator Regime** | Memory-Bandwidth-Bound Dominant | Compute-Bound Dominant |
| **Serving System Challenge** | Sustaining low ITL under high concurrency | Managing prefill compute spikes and TTFT |

In agentic systems, **the prefill phase accounts for 95% to 99% of all tokens processed**. As a result, the end-to-end execution profile is dominated by the compute-bound ingestion of massive prompt prefixes rather than the sequential output of long textual narratives.

#### End-to-End Latency Decomposition

To manage timeouts and ensure reliable agent execution loops, the host runtime models the end-to-end latency of a single model invocation ($T_{\text{invocation}}$) as a sum of four distinct components:

$$T_{\text{invocation}} = T_{\text{prep}} + T_{\text{queue}} + T_{\text{prefill}}(M) + \sum_{t=1}^K T_{\text{decode}}(t, S_t)$$

Where:
1. **$T_{\text{prep}}$ (Host CPU Overhead):** The time required by the host process to serialize structured context blocks, resolve working-set file state, tokenize Unicode strings into integer token sequences, and dispatch the HTTP/gRPC request payload across the network.
2. **$T_{\text{queue}}$ (Scheduling Queue Latency):** The latency spent resident in the serving engine's incoming request queue waiting for available execution slots and memory allocations on the accelerator.
3. **$T_{\text{prefill}}(M)$ (Prompt Ingestion Time / TTFT):** The compute-bound GEMM duration required to ingest $M$ staged tokens. For large $M$, this duration scales linearly with token count and model size:
   $$T_{\text{prefill}}(M) \approx \frac{2 \cdot P_{\text{params}} \cdot M}{P_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{GEMM}}}$$
   where $\eta_{\text{GEMM}}$ represents the hardware's numerical compute efficiency (typically $0.50 - 0.75$ on modern accelerators).
4. **$\sum_{t=1}^K T_{\text{decode}}(t, S_t)$ (Cumulative Decode Latency):** The total time spent in the autoregressive decode loop. Each step $t$ incurs a memory-shuttle latency that depends on the parameter shuttle floor and the expanding context sequence length $S_t = M + t$:
   $$T_{\text{decode}}(t, S_t) \approx \frac{P_{\text{params}} \cdot b_{\text{weight}} + Q_{\text{KV}}(S_t)}{\text{BW}_{\text{mem}} \cdot \eta_{\text{mem}}}$$
   where $\eta_{\text{mem}}$ represents sustained memory bus efficiency (typically $0.70 - 0.85$).

```
Total Invocation Latency T_invocation
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Host Prep │  Queue  │       Prefill Phase (GEMM)       │      Decode Phase (GEMV)       │
│  T_prep   │ T_queue │          T_prefill(M)            │       SUM(t=1..K) T_decode     │
├───────────┼─────────┼──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
│ CPU       │ Serving │ Accelerator Tensor Cores         │ Accelerator HBM Memory Bus     │
│ AST/BPE   │ FIFO    │ Compute-Bound Saturation         │ Memory-Bandwidth Shuttle Floor │
│ Serialization       │ Dominates Agent Invocation Time  │ Highly Serial, 40ms/tok Floor  │
└───────────┴─────────┴──────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
 0ms        15ms      85ms                             850ms                           1600ms
```

#### The Batching Dilemma: Single-Agent $B=1$ vs. Multi-Tenant Serving

In traditional throughput-oriented machine learning serving, runtimes mask memory-bandwidth bottlenecks through **batching**. If an inference server groups $B$ independent user requests into a single batch, the linear weight matrix $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$ loaded from HBM can be multiplied against a batch of $B$ activation vectors simultaneously:

$$\mathbf{Y}_{\text{batch}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\text{batch}} \quad \text{where} \quad \mathbf{X}_{\text{batch}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times B}$$

This transformation converts the memory-bound GEMV into a batched GEMM. The arithmetic intensity of the decode step scales directly with batch size $B$:

$$I_{\text{decode}}(B) \approx B \cdot I_{\text{decode}}(1) \approx B\text{ FLOP/byte}$$
