4. **Verified Downstream Task Completion Rate ($R_{\text{task}}$):** The fraction of tasks where the candidate action passes deterministic verification (e.g., hermetic test runner exit code $0$) under a fixed resource budget (such as an upper bound on total tokens $S_{\max} = M + K$ or wall-clock timeout $T_{\max}$).

### Architectural Comparison of Invocation Paradigms {#sec-vol3-interface-paradigms}

The physical mechanics of each interface paradigm impose distinct trade-offs between syntactic determinism, token efficiency, and accelerator execution profiles.

```
PARADIGM A: UNCONSTRAINED NATURAL LANGUAGE + REGEX
Host Prompt ──────► Accelerator (No Masking) ──────► Raw String Emitted ──────► Regex Match
                      • Fast ITL (No DFA)              • High Token Waste        • Parse Fragility
                      • Low Prefill Tax                • Hallucinated Tags       • AST Collisions

PARADIGM B: JSON SCHEMA-CONSTRAINED TOOL CALLING
Host Schema ──────► Accelerator (DFA Bitmask) ─────► Valid JSON Emitted ──────► Host JSON Deserializer
                      • Logit Masking Overhead         • Extreme Escape Tax      • 100% Syntax Validity
                      • High Prefill Schema Tax        • Rigid Syntax Padding    • Risk of Empty Payloads

PARADIGM C: GRAMMAR-MASKED SEARCH/REPLACE DIFFS
Host Format ──────► Accelerator (Diff Grammar) ────► Search/Replace Block ────► Host Patch Engine
                      • Minimal Masking Overhead       • Zero JSON Escaping      • Exact In-Place Edits
                      • Ultra-Low Delta K              • Dense Information       • High Task Success
```

#### Unconstrained Natural Language with Regex Parsing

Under unconstrained generation, the neural processor emits tokens according to its raw language modeling objective without decode-time logit intervention. The host runtime instructs the model to wrap structured actions in markdown code fences or custom XML-like tags (e.g., `<tool_call>{"name": "edit", ...}</tool_call>`).

- *Mechanical Advantages:* Zero accelerator compute overhead for logit masking ($t_{\text{mask}} = 0$). The decode phase proceeds at the theoretical HBM bandwidth saturation speed ($\text{ITL} \approx \text{ITL}_{\text{shuttle}}$).
- *Systems Failure Modes:* The interface suffers from severe syntactic entropy. Because subword tokenizers fracture syntax delimiters across token boundaries, the model routinely emits malformed tags, forgets closing delimiters, or interpolates conversational commentary inside payload bodies. When evaluated on complex multi-argument actions, $R_{\text{syntax}}$ degrades precipitously ($60\%\text{--}80\%$), requiring the host runtime to waste trajectory cycles executing multi-turn error correction prompts.

#### JSON Schema-Constrained Tool Calling

JSON schema enforcement compiles a structural specification (e.g., JSON Schema or Pydantic model) into a regular grammar or pushdown automaton. At each step $k$ of the decode loop, the accelerator runtime projects the current parser state onto vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$, constructing a bitmask that forces logits of illegal tokens to $-\infty$.

- *Mechanical Advantages:* Perfect structural compliance ($R_{\text{syntax}} = 100\%$). The host runtime is guaranteed that emitted sequences deserialize into valid JSON objects matching the target type signature.
- *Systems Failure Modes:* The guarantee of syntactic validity incurs substantial systems taxes. First, prompt token inflation $\Delta M$ escalates because comprehensive JSON schema definitions must be injected into the system prompt, consuming prefill compute and displacing working memory. Second, decode token inflation $\Delta K$ is severe: JSON requires escaping internal quotes, formatting newlines as `\n`, repeating structural keys (`"path"`, `"replacement_chunk"`), and wrapping code in strings. Most critically, grammar masking guarantees *structure*, not *content*; when constrained to emit a valid schema under high epistemic uncertainty, the model frequently emits syntactically flawless but operationally vacuous payloads (e.g., empty patch strings or truncated functions).

#### Grammar-Masked Search/Replace Diffs

Grammar-masked diff interfaces replace generic serialization schemas with domain-specific grammars tailored to code editing and file mutations. The model is constrained to emit an exact search block followed by a replacement block:

```
<<<<<<< SEARCH
def process_event(event_id: str) -> None:
    record = fetch_record(event_id)
=======
def process_event(event_id: str) -> None:
    if not event_id:
        return
    record = fetch_record(event_id)
>>>>>>> REPLACE
```

The grammar enforces the sequence of marker tokens (`<<<<<<< SEARCH`, `=======`, `>>>>>>> REPLACE`) and allows arbitrary unescaped code inside the block bodies.

- *Mechanical Advantages:* High information density. The model emits raw code tokens without JSON string escaping, quote serialization, or nested indentation overhead. Token decode overhead is strictly bounded to the edited region plus minimal framing markers ($\Delta K \le 20\text{ tokens}$).
- *Systems Failure Modes:* The interface depends entirely on the accuracy of the search block. If the model emits a search chunk that does not match the target file uniquely, the host-side patch engine fails to locate the target hunk, yielding an application-level match failure despite valid grammar framing.

| Invocation Interface Paradigm | Structural Validity ($R_{\text{syntax}}$) | Prefix Overhead ($\Delta M$) | Output Token Overhead ($\Delta K$) | Serving Compute Profile | Primary Systems Failure Bottleneck |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Free-Form NL + Regex** | Low to Moderate ($60\%\text{--}82\%$) | Minimal ($0\text{--}50\text{ tok}$) | Unbounded ($100\text{--}800\text{ tok}$) | Unconstrained GEMV; $t_{\text{mask}} = 0$ | Delimiter hallucination; parse failures; conversation leakage |
| **JSON Schema Tool Calling** | Deterministic ($100\%$) | High ($150\text{--}600\text{ tok}$) | High ($\Delta K \approx 1.4\text{--}2.2\times$) | Bitmask overhead ($t_{\text{mask}} \approx 1.5\text{--}4.0\text{ ms}$); DFA state tracking | High decode latency; JSON escape inflation; vacuous payloads |
| **Grammar Search/Replace** | Near-Deterministic ($98\%\text{--}100\%$) | Low ($40\text{--}80\text{ tok}$) | Minimal ($\Delta K \le 20\text{ tok}$) | Specialized marker masking; zero JSON serialization | Search target mismatch; multi-occurrence ambiguity in host file |

: Quantitative Evaluation of Invocation Interface Paradigms. {#tbl-vol3-interface-evaluation}

### Core Evaluation Metrics and Systems Trade-Offs {#sec-vol3-interface-metrics}

When evaluating invocation interfaces, the central systems trade-off is the tension between **decoding efficiency** and **downstream task verification**. Because autoregressive token generation sits on the physical HBM bandwidth floor, every additional token emitted by an interface imposes a linear latency penalty and increases the cumulative risk of stochastic sequence degradation.

#### The Token Overhead Tax

Consider a task requiring a host-side modification: updating a 5-line bug fix inside a 500-line Python module ($S_{\text{file}} = 2{,}500\text{ tokens}$). An agent operating system can interface with the neural coprocessor through three distinct edit abstractions:

1. **Full File Regeneration:** The interface instructs the model to rewrite the entire target file containing the fix.
2. **JSON Patch Serialization:** The interface forces the model to emit a JSON payload containing file path, start line, end line, and the replacement code wrapped in an escaped string.
3. **Targeted Search/Replace Chunk:** The interface enforces a grammar diff specifying only the lines to be replaced and their immediate surrounding context.

The physical implications of these three paradigms are starkly exposed by hardware Roofline modeling.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Sizing the Token Overhead Tax Across Code Editing Paradigms"}
**Problem Statement:** An agent runtime running on a single NVIDIA H100 SXM5 node ($80\text{ GiB}$ HBM3, $\text{BW}_{\text{mem}} = 3.35\text{ TB/s}$) invokes a quantized Llama-3-70B model in FP8 ($P = 70 \times 10^9\text{ parameters}$, occupying $70\text{ GB}$ of memory). The runtime must apply a 5-line patch to a 500-line Python file ($2{,}500\text{ tokens}$).

Evaluate the decode latency, HBM parameter shuttling volume, and sequence drift vulnerability across the three interface paradigms:
1. *Full File Rewrite:* Emits the complete file ($K_1 = 2{,}500\text{ tokens}$).
2. *JSON Patch Schema:* Emits JSON metadata and escaped code ($K_2 = 450\text{ tokens}$).
3. *Search/Replace Diff:* Emits search block, markers, and replacement lines ($K_3 = 75\text{ tokens}$).

---

**Step 1: Physical Parameter Shuttle Floor per Token**
During single-batch token decode ($B=1$), the arithmetic intensity sits well below the H100 saturation boundary ($I \ll I_{\text{sat}} = 295.2\text{ FLOP/byte}$). Every token decode requires streaming the entire model parameter tensor from HBM into the Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs).

The theoretical memory-read time per token is:
$$t_{\text{shuttle}} = \frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{BW}_{\text{mem}}} = \frac{70 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}}{3.35 \times 10^{12}\text{ bytes/s}} \approx 20.89\text{ ms/token}$$

Accounting for CUDA kernel launch overhead, KV-cache lookup, and sampling latency, the sustained per-token decode latency on the host serving engine is calibrated at $\text{ITL} \approx 26.0\text{ ms/token}$ (yielding an effective decode throughput of $\approx 38.46\text{ tokens/s}$).

---

**Step 2: Decode Latency and HBM Data Volume Calculation**

*Paradigm 1: Full File Rewrite ($K_1 = 2{,}500\text{ tokens}$)*
- **Wall-Clock Decode Time:**
  $$T_{\text{decode}, 1} = 2{,}500\text{ tokens} \times 0.026\text{ s/token} = 65.0\text{ s}$$
- **HBM Parameter Shuttling Volume:**
  $$V_{\text{HBM}, 1} = 2{,}500 \times 70\text{ GB} = 175{,}000\text{ GB} = 175.0\text{ TB}$$

*Paradigm 2: JSON Patch Schema ($K_2 = 450\text{ tokens}$)*
- **Wall-Clock Decode Time:**
  $$T_{\text{decode}, 2} = 450\text{ tokens} \times 0.026\text{ s/token} = 11.7\text{ s} \approx 12.0\text{ s}$$
- **HBM Parameter Shuttling Volume:**
  $$V_{\text{HBM}, 2} = 450 \times 70\text{ GB} = 31{,}500\text{ GB} = 31.5\text{ TB}$$

*Paradigm 3: Search/Replace Diff ($K_3 = 75\text{ tokens}$)*
- **Wall-Clock Decode Time:**
  $$T_{\text{decode}, 3} = 75\text{ tokens} \times 0.024\text{ s/token} = 1.80\text{ s}$$
  *(Note: Search/replace avoids complex schema DFA bitmask traversal, reducing per-token overhead to $\approx 24.0\text{ ms/token}$).*
- **HBM Parameter Shuttling Volume:**
  $$V_{\text{HBM}, 3} = 75 \times 70\text{ GB} = 5{,}250\text{ GB} = 5.25\text{ TB}$$

---

**Step 3: Stochastic Error Drift Accumulation**
Autoregressive decoding is a causal Markov chain. At each step $k$, there exists an empirical probability $\epsilon$ that the model samples a degenerated token, hallucinated syntax, or unrequested modification in existing code. The probability $P_{\text{clean}}$ of generating an uncorrupted sequence across $K$ consecutive tokens scales inversely with length:
$$P_{\text{clean}} = (1 - \epsilon)^K$$

Assuming a high-fidelity per-token non-drift probability $(1 - \epsilon) = 0.9999$ ($\epsilon = 10^{-4}$):
- **Full File ($K=2{,}500$):**
  $$P_{\text{clean}, 1} = (0.9999)^{2500} \approx 77.88\%$$
  *(Over a 22% probability of introducing an unprompted syntax error, dropped comment, or hallucinated change elsewhere in the file).*
- **JSON Patch ($K=450$):**
  $$P_{\text{clean}, 2} = (0.9999)^{450} \approx 95.60\%$$
- **Search/Replace ($K=75$):**
  $$P_{\text{clean}, 3} = (0.9999)^{75} \approx 99.25\%$$

---

**Systems Conclusion:**
Choosing the search/replace diff interface over full-file regeneration reduces accelerator memory bus traffic by $33.3\times$ ($5.25\text{ TB}$ vs. $175.0\text{ TB}$), slashes decode wall-clock time from over a minute ($65.0\text{ s}$) to interactive speed ($1.8\text{ s}$), and raises the probability of an uncorrupted modification from $77.88\%$ to $99.25\%$.
:::

#### The Masking Latency Tax vs. Re-Invocation Tax

A common systems design dilemma is whether the latency tax of accelerator-side grammar masking ($t_{\text{mask}}$) is justified compared to unconstrained decoding paired with host-side retry loops.

Let $T_{\text{unconstrained}}$ represent the duration of an unmasked model call, with structural validity rate $R_{\text{syntax}} < 1$. When a parse failure occurs, the host runtime must re-stage the context and execute an error correction retry, incurring an additional invocation penalty:
$$\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{unconstrained}}] = T_{\text{unconstrained}} + (1 - R_{\text{syntax}}) \left( T_{\text{retry}} + T_{\text{host\_reparse}} \right)$$

Under grammar-constrained decoding, $R_{\text{syntax}} = 1.0$, but each token decode step incurs a bitmask projection overhead $t_{\text{mask}}$:
$$T_{\text{constrained}} = \text{TTFT}(M) + \sum_{k=1}^K \left( \text{ITL}_{\text{shuttle}} + t_{\text{mask}}(k) \right)$$

On modern GPU serving engines (e.g., vLLM with Outlines or XGrammar), the grammar DFA is pre-compiled into a trie index and cached on device memory. For standard JSON schemas or regular expressions, the GPU kernel overhead is bounded:
$$t_{\text{mask}} \le 0.5\text{--}2.0\text{ ms/token}$$

Because the baseline memory shuttle floor for 70B models is large ($\text{ITL}_{\text{shuttle}} \approx 20\text{--}26\text{ ms}$), a $1.5\text{ ms}$ masking tax represents an expansion of only $\approx 6\%$ in per-token decode latency. Conversely, a single failed turn requiring a re-invocation retry forces a complete prompt re-prefill ($M$ tokens) and a secondary decode phase ($K$ tokens), adding tens of seconds to the trajectory.

Thus, from a systems queueing and latency perspective:
$$\text{Cost}(\text{Grammar Masking}) \ll \text{Cost}(\text{Host Re-invocation})$$
Hardware-level grammar constraints are almost always computationally cheaper than host-level retry loops, provided the grammar does not force excessive output token expansion ($\Delta K$).

### Closing the Verification Loop Under Budget Parity {#sec-vol3-interface-selection}

The ultimate measure of an invocation interface is its **Verified Task Completion Rate ($R_{\text{task}}$) under strict resource parity**. An interface cannot be declared superior simply because it generates cleaner code or achieves zero schema errors; it must convert a fixed compute budget into verified task solutions.

```
                         EQUAL RESOURCE BUDGET: 100,000 TOKENS
                                          │
                  ┌───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
                  ▼                                               ▼
     PARADIGM B: JSON SCHEMA EDITING                 PARADIGM C: SEARCH/REPLACE DIFFS
  • Avg Tokens / Action: 650 tokens               • Avg Tokens / Action: 110 tokens
  • Total Trajectory Steps: ~153 turns            • Total Trajectory Steps: ~909 turns
  • High Schema Overhead                          • Minimal Framing Overhead
  • Trajectory Budget Exhausted Quickly           • Extensive Exploration Budget Available
                  │                                               │
                  ▼                                               ▼
       R_task = 34.2% Passed                           R_task = 58.7% Passed
```

When multi-file software engineering tasks (such as SWE-bench benchmarks) are evaluated under a fixed token allocation (e.g., $100{,}000\text{ tokens}$ total trajectory budget):

1. **The Budget Exhaustion Failure Mode:** Interfaces with high $\Delta M$ and $\Delta K$ (such as JSON-wrapped full file outputs) consume the trajectory's token budget in a small number of turns. If the initial modification contains a semantic defect, the runtime lacks the remaining token budget to run the compiler, ingest the error trace, and attempt a secondary fix.
2. **The Exploration Advantage of Compact Interfaces:** Compact interfaces (such as grammar-masked search/replace diffs) minimize both prefill overhead and decode serialization. By reducing per-action token expenditure from $650\text{ tokens}$ to $110\text{ tokens}$, the agent operating system achieves a $5.9\times$ expansion in available exploratory turns under the identical hardware budget. The runtime can afford multiple test executions, compiler cycles, and refinement iterations.

```
                 SYSTEMS INTERFACE TRADEOFF ENVELOPE
    100% ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                   [Search/Replace]     │
         │                                          ▲             │
R_task   │                                         ╱              │
(Task    │                                        ╱               │
Success) │                     [JSON Schema]     ╱                │
         │                           ▲          ╱                 │
         │                          ╱          ╱                  │
         │                         ╱          ╱                   │
         │      [Free-form NL]    ╱          ╱                    │
         │            ▲          ╱          ╱                     │
      0% └────────────┴─────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────┘
         0%                                                    100%
                          Token Packing Efficiency
                     (Payload Tokens / Total Emitted Tokens)
```

In accordance with the Saltzer and Kaashoek End-to-End Argument, lower-layer interface mechanics—whether regex parsers, JSON schema bitmasks, or diff engines—are merely mechanical adapters. They enforce structural invariants at the communication boundary. However, structural perfection does not imply application correctness. True systems reliability emerges only when the invocation interface is paired with authoritative host-level verification: compiling emitted code, running sealed regression tests, and inspecting execution exit codes.

Having established the quantitative trade-offs of the model invocation boundary—from tokenization and Roofline accelerator physics to grammar constraints and interface benchmarking—systems engineers must be vigilant against recurring industry misconceptions. When treating a non-deterministic neural network as an unprivileged computing element, several widespread architectural intuitions collapse under physical measurement.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-processor-fallacies}

Architectural intuitions derived from deterministic CPU pipelines or standard microservice architectures frequently break down when applied to neural processing cores. Treating the foundation model as a generic remote procedure call obscures the physical accelerator bottlenecks, communication contracts, and verification boundaries required to operate a dependable host runtime. Systems engineers building agentic runtimes must confront the following critical fallacies and implementation pitfalls.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *One model response is one forward pass.*

A common architectural misconception is to model an inference call as an atomic functional evaluation—analogous to calling an external library function or issuing a single database query. Under this mental model, the host runtime dispatches an input buffer and receives a generated response from a single execution pass through the model's neural network layers.

In physical reality, the foundation model invocation boundary is fundamentally split into two computationally and structurally distinct phases: parallel prompt prefill and serialized autoregressive decode.

1. **Prompt Prefill:** The staged sequence of $M$ prompt tokens is processed concurrently in a single computational pass. Because all $M$ tokens are known *a priori*, the attention and feed-forward projections execute as dense Matrix-Matrix multiplications (GEMM). This phase achieves high arithmetic intensity ($I \gg I_{\text{sat}}$), saturating the GPU Tensor Cores at compute-bound efficiency to produce the initial Key-Value (KV) cache activations.
2. **Autoregressive Decode:** Emitting a response sequence of $K$ tokens requires an irreducibly sequential loop of exactly $K$ discrete forward passes. Because token generation is causally autoregressive—each new token $y_t$ depends conditionally on all preceding tokens $y_{<t}$—token $y_t$ cannot be computed until token $y_{t-1}$ has been sampled, dequantized, and appended to the KV cache.

At batch size $B=1$ (the operating regime of a single interactive agent trajectory), every individual decode step executes as a memory-bound Matrix-Vector multiplication (GEMV). The entire parameter tensor matrix $\mathbf{W}$ across all $L$ layers must be fetched from off-chip High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), shuttled across the memory bus into on-chip SRAM registers, and contracted against the single active token vector.

For a $70\text{B}$ parameter model in 16-bit precision ($\approx 140\text{ GB}$ of weights) hosted on an NVIDIA H100 SXM5 accelerator ($3.35\text{ TB/s}$ HBM3 bandwidth), the physical parameter shuttle imposes a strict latency floor per token:
$$t_{\text{token}} \ge \frac{140\text{ GB}}{3.35\text{ TB/s}} \approx 41.8\text{ ms}$$
This limits single-batch generation throughput to $\le 23.9\text{ tokens/s}$. Producing a response of $K = 1{,}024$ tokens does not execute one forward pass; it executes $1$ prefill pass followed by $1{,}024$ sequential forward passes, shuttling:
$$140\text{ GB} \times 1{,}024 \approx 143.36\text{ TB}$$
of model weights across the accelerator memory bus.

**Architectural Defense:** Runtimes must never treat model invocations as atomic $O(1)$ operations. Schedulers must model execution as an $O(K)$ iterative loop. Host systems should consume token streams incrementally via Server-Sent Events (SSE) to overlap host parsing with accelerator decode, enforce Inter-Token Latency (`ITL`) watchdogs rather than coarse request-level timeouts, and support immediate generation preemption as soon as stopping criteria or structural syntax violations are detected.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall:** *Treating a completed invocation as a completed task.*

In conventional client-server architectures, an HTTP `200 OK` status code combined with a payload status such as `finish_reason: "stop"` or `status: "COMPLETED"` indicates that the requested operation finished successfully. Runtimes that carry this assumption into agent system design conflate transport termination with task completion, advancing the trajectory control plane without verifying whether the model's emitted proposal is functional or even valid.

An invocation completion signal certifies only that the serving engine's autoregressive decode loop terminated cleanly—either by sampling an end-of-sequence token (`<|endoftext|>`), encountering a registered stop sequence, or exhausting the token budget. It provides zero guarantees regarding semantic validity, environment applicability, or algorithmic correctness.

Under the principle of Zero Ambient Authority ($A=0$), a model output is merely an unverified proposal held in host escrow. The emitted payload may:
- Assert that a non-existent file was created or modified.
- Generate synthetic code containing subtle syntax errors, broken imports, or hallucinated third-party dependencies.
- Fabricate plausible but incorrect command-line flags that trigger silent runtime failures.
- Produce patch diffs that fail mechanical `patch --check` verification.

Conflating invocation completion with task completion violates the Saltzer and Kaashoek End-to-End Argument. A transport protocol cannot certify application correctness.

**Architectural Mitigation:** The host runtime must decouple the *Invocation Lifecycle* from the *Task State Machine*. A successful invocation status (`INVOCATION_SUCCESS`) merely delivers candidate bytes into the host environment. The runtime must route candidate proposals through an authoritative verification pipeline:
1. *Static Verification:* In-memory AST parsing, type checking, and schema validation.
2. *Environment Mediation:* Verifying that referenced files, directories, and capabilities exist in the host filesystem.
3. *Dynamic Execution:* Executing proposed operations within an isolated sandbox and measuring deterministic outcomes (compiler exit codes, linter reports, and sealed unit test suites).

A task advances to `TASK_COMPLETE` if and only if deterministic external verification oracles return success.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *Valid JSON means a safe and correct tool call.*

With the development of grammar-constrained decoding engines (such as Outlines, XGrammar, and LM-Format-Enforcer), serving runtimes can guarantee that model emissions adhere strictly to a specified schema. By compiling Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) or JSON schemas into deterministic finite automata (DFAs) and masking illegal token logits to $-\infty$ during each decode step, the engine ensures that emitted text is $100\%$ syntactically valid JSON. Systems engineers often fall into the trap of assuming that syntactic validity guarantees operational safety and semantic correctness.

Grammar constraints operate exclusively at the *lexical and syntactic layers* of the Chomsky hierarchy. The accelerator's logit mask guarantees character-level structural compliance (braces match, required field keys appear, string literals escape correctly, and numeric types parse), but it possesses zero awareness of semantic meaning or execution context:
- **Contextual Incoherence:** A schema requiring `{"path": "<string>"}` guarantees that a string is emitted, but cannot ensure that the path `/opt/runtime/config.json` exists or is accessible.
- **Relational Invalidation:** A tool schema requiring `{"start_line": int, "end_line": int}` cannot enforce the semantic invariant $\text{end\_line} \ge \text{start\_line}$ across independent integer token emissions without intractable grammar state explosion.
- **Privilege and Safety Violations:** A schema for shell execution will happily emit `{"command": "rm -rf / --no-preserve-root"}` with flawless syntactic conformance.
- **Schema-Induced Hallucinations:** When an agent encounters an edge case that falls outside the expressive bounds of a rigid schema, logit masking suppresses explanatory or refusal tokens (such as `"I cannot proceed because..."`). Forcing probability mass onto the restricted schema compels the model to emit a high-confidence, syntactically perfect hallucination—an effect known as the *Mars Multiple-Choice Exam* dilemma.

**Architectural Defense:** Treat grammar-guided decoding strictly as a serialization adapter that eliminates downstream JSON parsing failures at the transport boundary. The host runtime must never grant execution authority based on schema compliance alone. Every parsed payload must undergo three independent validation stages prior to dispatch:
1. *Semantic Range Validation:* Validating value bounds, relational constraints, and invariant logic using host-level validation libraries.
2. *State Grounding Checks:* Authoritatively verifying the existence and state of referenced files, repositories, or network resources.
3. *Capability Mediation:* Enforcing security policies within an isolated sandbox boundary, intercepting destructive or out-of-scope system calls regardless of how cleanly formatted the JSON appears.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall:** *Collapsing incomplete, refusal, and transport failures into a generic retry loop.*

A standard resilience pattern in distributed systems is to wrap remote procedure calls in a generic retry wrapper (e.g., using exponential backoff) that catches all exceptions and resubmits the request. When applied indiscriminately to the model invocation boundary, this pattern degrades agent reliability, wastes compute budgets, and frequently sends the runtime into unrecoverable failure loops.

Failures at the model invocation boundary originate from fundamentally distinct root causes that require divergent mitigation strategies:

1. **Transient Infrastructure Faults:** Network timeouts, HTTP `429 Too Many Requests`, HTTP `503 Service Unavailable`, or transient accelerator memory fragmentation (`CUDA OOM` under peak batch sizes). These are non-semantic system faults. Retrying the identical request with exponential backoff and randomized jitter is the correct recovery strategy.
2. **Context and Generation Truncation (`finish_reason: "length"`):** The decode loop was terminated because the generation hit the token ceiling $K_{\max}$, or the staged prompt exceeded the context window $S_{\max}$. The returned payload is an incomplete, fractured prefix (often terminating mid-string or mid-JSON token). Resubmitting the exact same prompt with identical parameters deterministically reproduces the exact same truncation, burning tokens without making progress.
3. **Safety and Policy Refusals (`finish_reason: "content_filter"`):** The model or serving guardrail actively suppressed the generation due to policy triggers. Re-submitting the identical prompt will trigger the identical refusal.
4. **Grammar Deadlocks:** The generation entered a state where all tokens permitted by the grammar DFA have near-zero probability mass in the base model distribution, causing the engine to emit degenerate loops or terminate early. Resubmitting with identical parameters reproduces the deadlock.

**Architectural Mitigation:** The host runtime must construct a strongly typed `InvocationStatusEnvelope` that categorizes failures into explicit error classes with targeted recovery paths:
- `TRANSIENT_INFRA_ERROR`: Retry with exponential backoff, jitter, and circuit-breaker monitoring.
- `BUDGET_TRUNCATION`: Do not retry blindly. Escalate the generation ceiling $K_{\max}$, or trigger a context compaction pass to prune prompt tokens before re-invoking.
- `POLICY_REFUSAL`: Terminate the immediate execution branch, log an auditable security event, and route the trajectory to a fallback model or an administrative escalation handler.
- `SYNTACTIC_DEADLOCK / VALIDATION_FAILURE`: Intercept the specific failure trace (e.g., the JSON parser or linter error message) and inject it into the next turn's prompt context as an explicit observation. This allows the model to inspect its previous failure and adjust its generation strategy in the subsequent invocation.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *Models have internal hardware traps.*

Software engineers accustomed to systems programming often assume that an LLM possesses an internal execution engine analogous to a microprocessor—complete with status flags, illegal instruction traps, divide-by-zero faults, and memory segmentation mechanisms. When a model outputs malformed syntax, references nonexistent variables, or hallucinates an incorrect reasoning trace, developers frequently describe the model as having "errored," "faulted," or "crashed" internally.

In physical reality, an autoregressive neural network has no program counter, no stack pointer, no interrupt vector table, and no Memory Management Unit (MMU). Mathematically, a transformer forward pass is a continuous, differentiable cascade of dense tensor contractions and non-linear activations:
$$\mathbf{z}_l = \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x}_{l-1} + \text{Attention}(\mathbf{x}_{l-1}))$$
$$\mathbf{x}_l = \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{z}_l + \text{FFN}(\mathbf{z}_l))$$

At no point in this computational graph can an arithmetic overflow, an illegal memory access, or an instruction fault occur. The network always computes real-valued logits $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$ and normalizes them into a categorical probability distribution via softmax:
$$P(y_t \mid y_{<t}) = \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{z} / \tau)$$

When a model outputs syntactically invalid Python code or fabricates a nonexistent Git commit hash, every floating-point operation on the accelerator's Tensor Cores executed with complete arithmetic success. The "error" exists purely in the external semantic interpretation of the sampled token sequence. The neural processor cannot "know" that it emitted an error; it simply sampled tokens from a conditioned probability distribution.

**Architectural Defense:** Because the accelerator core possesses no internal exception-handling or fault-trapping hardware, the host agent runtime must provide the entire supervisor, MMU, and trap-handling infrastructure externally.

The runtime must act as the supervisor kernel to the unprivileged neural coprocessor:
- It intercepts raw output token streams.
- It parses them against formal ABI definitions.
- It traps syntax errors, invalid references, and security violations using deterministic host-side tooling (compilers, linters, schemas, and sandboxed execution environments).
- It reflects these execution traps back to the model as structured environmental feedback, establishing the closed-loop control required for reliable system behavior.
:::

Dismantling these architectural fallacies grounds the engineering of agent runtimes in the physical realities of the stochastic computer. The foundation model is neither an all-knowing agent capable of certifying its own correctness, nor is it an ordinary CPU equipped with internal fault traps. It is an unprivileged, non-deterministic inference coprocessor whose memory bandwidth boundaries, serialization costs, and output proposals must be strictly governed by the host operating system.

## Summary {#sec-vol3-processor-summary}

A single model invocation is a bounded, learned statistical mapping that transforms staged token sequences into candidate continuations via compute-bound prompt prefill and memory-bandwidth-bound autoregressive decode. Under zero ambient authority ($A=0$), evaluating a neural network alters zero host bits and emits candidate token sequences without any inherent guarantee of empirical truth, semantic correctness, or system safety. Traditional computing systems build on deterministic processors with inspectable registers and hardware-enforced fault traps; the stochastic processor provides none of these guarantees. Left unmediated, raw token generation produces silent semantic corruptions, unbounded execution latency, and uncontrolled resource consumption. Governing the invocation boundary requires the host runtime to function as an authoritative supervisor: staging prompt tokens, enforcing strict token and latency ceilings ($S_{\max}$, $T_{\max}$), constraining output syntax via decode-time logit masking, and intercepting output proposals within a typed, mediated interface.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Core Systems Principles of the Model Invocation Boundary"}

* **Tokens are discrete integer symbols and vocabulary gather indices.** Subword tokenization via Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) is a statistical byte serializer between raw strings and integer identifiers. Because vocabulary merges follow corpus statistics rather than formal language syntax, token boundaries fracture programming language keywords, indentation blocks, and structured schemas. This creates an impedance mismatch with Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) and imposes a measurable serialization tax on structured tool interfaces.
* **Autoregressive decode forms an irreducibly serial causal dependency chain on accelerator memory.** While prompt prefill processes all $M$ staged tokens in parallel via dense Matrix-Matrix multiplication (GEMM), generating $K$ output tokens requires $K$ sequential forward passes. Each generated token $y_t$ depends causally on all preceding tokens, bounding single-trajectory serving latency along an irreducibly serial $O(K)$ execution path regardless of available parallel hardware cores.
* **Single-batch agent decode is memory-bandwidth bound at the parameter shuttle floor.** At batch size $B=1$, token decode executes Matrix-Vector operations (GEMV) characterized by low arithmetic intensity ($I \ll I_{\text{sat}}$). The accelerator must shuttle its entire parameter weight matrix from High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) into on-chip cache registers to emit a single token, stranding the vast majority of peak tensor arithmetic throughput and locking per-token latency to the physical memory bandwidth ceiling.
* **Likelihood and structural validity do not establish truth, safety, or authority.** Autoregressive sampling optimizes statistical sequence likelihood under learned weights, not operational correctness. Constraining output syntax through decode-time logit masking guarantees that emitted bytes conform to formal context-free grammars or JSON schemas, but grammatical validity provides zero verification of factual truth, file existence, or execution invariants.
* **The invocation contract must enforce explicit budgets, early streaming cancellation, and normalized outcome envelopes.** Model serving cannot be modeled as an unconstrained remote procedure call. The host runtime must specify strict input token budgets ($M$), maximum generation limits ($K$), and wall-clock deadlines ($T_{\max}$). It must support early streaming cancellation via flow-control traps when generation violates invariants, and normalize all execution terminations into a strict four-state envelope: COMPLETED, TRUNCATED, REFUSED, or TRANSPORT_FAILURE.
* **Candidate generations must be quarantined in host memory escrow until verified by external deterministic gates.** Because the neural core operates under the Fail-Plausible fault model, candidate proposals cannot directly mutate host state. The runtime supervisor must hold proposed diffs, commands, and parameter blocks in memory escrow, validating them against external static analyzers, linters, and schema checkers before committing changes to persistent environments.

:::

These principles establish the fundamental division of labor in the stochastic computer: the foundation model serves as an unprivileged inference coprocessor whose physical latency is constrained by memory bus physics, while the host runtime operates as the supervisor kernel that establishes bounded operational safety. In accordance with Saltzer, Reed, and Clark's end-to-end argument, low-level decode mechanisms enforce structural syntactic boundaries, but substantive correctness cannot be certified by the neural core. Operational dependability emerges solely when the host runtime isolates candidate proposals under zero ambient authority, bounds execution resources through explicit contracts, and verifies every proposed transition against deterministic host-side checks.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From One Candidate to Deliberate Computation"}

A single model invocation produces exactly one unprivileged, stochastic candidate sequence. When that sequence is ambiguous, incomplete, or fails host-side verification, simply re-issuing the prompt with identical parameters compounds failure modes. In classical systems design, when a single speculative operation yields low confidence, the architecture introduces branching, speculative execution, or multi-path verification. Chapter 03 examines how the runtime allocates additional inference-time compute—structuring sequential deliberation, tree search, and verification oracles—to transform stochastic candidate proposals into dependable systems outcomes before touching external environment state.

:::
